items.title: [Read-Along] The Odyssey (W.H.D Rouse transl.), Remarks
items.text:
# Some thoughts

Here I am proposing doing something maybe a little juvenile, so you are free to be all growed up and just observe. 

Here is also my attempt at changing @denlillaapan 's mind about stories. Although I know he's reviewed fiction here, I am not convinced he has done so for any reason other than he thought it might be a good way to seduce me to zap his posts in the territory. 

That aside, my other-half--who works arguably harder than I do--has been having trouble sleeping, so I have offered to read to her a bedtime story so that she stays away from her screen.  We picked the Odyssey and we have just finished Book 1. So far, the results have been positive.

# The translation

Selected edition: *[The Odyssey, Homed. Translated by W.H.D. Rouse.](https*://a.co/d/08xXX1xi)*

After toying with the idea of not watching the film, and reading the poem instead, I came across the translation of [W.H.D Rouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._H._D._Rouse), which--to me--strikes a fair balance in using lay-person friendly language while, at the same time, is uncontroversial in its treatment of the classical ethics that readers often look for in the poem. 

The Odyssey, in it's heyday, wouldn't have been thought of as a 'book' per se, but a poetic performance. Kind of like how you watch Netflix before you doze off to sleep, except, to my knowledge, there was no internet in the classical period of Greek history. Bards performed sections of this epic poem, which had to be committed to memory, for every day folk like you and me. This oral tradition of the poem means that it should be made accessible to as many people as possible, which I think this translation is. 

# A read-along

I have chosen to call it a read-along, because you can contribute as well as just observe and learn about the poem. It will not follow book-club logic. There is no schedule. Anyone can contribute at any time. Just get a copy, read a chapter (preferably without skipping ahead), and then post your summary. 

A note on pacing: my wife and I do not have a long attention span, may have missed a day here and there, and so it took us a week to get through book 1 (11 pages). I think those who wish to read along will find this pace amenable. 
# Read-along summary suggestions  

As I do this, I may have other ideas, but for each "Book" I am thinking the following would be nice to have: 

- a short summary of the story 
- a key character list (including gods, humans, giants, etc.)
- key places mentioned 
- some thoughts/questions

If you do participate, I may catalogue it in a pinned post on ~the_stacker_muse territory. In that case, I will use the following naming convention: 

> [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, <Book Number>

That way at the end we'll have a neat looking list of posts to compile and passers-by can peruse and learn about the epic poem. 

Also, please feel free to cross-post in ~BooksAndArticles (I hear there are some pretty juicy rewards sloshing around over there). 

# Join me 

If you are interested and would like to get your hands on a copy, you have a few days before I update you on Book 1. 

So what are you waiting for, get off your damn government-surveilling, blue-light radiating, endocrine-disrupting smartphones and join me as I read the greatest story ever told.

items.title: Slowly Exiting the Fiat World with Bitcoin e-SIM
items.text:
Recently, I noticed my current SIM card subscription is about to expire, so I checked how much the new subscription will cost. The SIM provider has jacked up the price over the years in the name of giving you MORE internet data, which I barely use. I don't really need 50 GB each month or 2000 mins for calls. *It's really important to know what you actually need, because the fiat world loves to package things you don't need.* So I was thinking maybe switch to prepaid, pay-as-I-go, and I had to call the call center *three* times to get it done. **Only after going through things like this do you really appreciate how much better the experience is with Bitcoin e-SIM services.**

I would like to share the current Bitcoin e-SIM options (mainly for internet and receiving messages) and my experience here.

***

### [**Silent link**](https://silent.link)

No KYC, no email needed. I have been using Silent Link for at least two years, and I've traveled to different countries with it. You are literally able to access the local internet the second you land, which is really handy for travelers!

Another bonus: even in places where one local provider is weak, you can manually switch to another, which basically means you can choose the provider whenever instead of locking into one like in the fiat world.

**Pricing**: $9 for data only, with a $5 initial balance.

![](https://m.stacker.news/155973)

The paying experience is great. Onchain and LN payment available. It redirects to a unique link with a QR code after you pay, then you just scan it with your phone, super easy. **Don't forget to bookmark the unique link for later top-ups.** Top-up is super simple too: just go back to the unique link you bookmarked, create an invoice, and pay.

To check how much money is left, dial \*187#.

![](https://m.stacker.news/155974)

Silent Link also offers number rental (US numbers only). I tried that too, but the number I got couldn't register for some apps, so I stopped using it.

***

### [**Nadanada**](https://nadanada.me/)

No KYC, no email needed. Nadanada has more services than Silent Link, including VPN, e-SIM, disposable numbers, and number rental; I tested the 3-month rental number, and I quite liked the overall experience, especially the part that you don't need to download another App so to receive messages, all you need is simply log back in to the link, which is super cool!

**Pricing**

3-month UK rental number: $12; 12-month UK rental number: $44.

![](https://m.stacker.news/155975)

It also redirects to a unique link after payment, don't forget to bookmark it for renew or to receive messages.

I think Nadanada is especially good for business. Don't use Google Voice or anything like that, because they would take the number back for no reason. One more detail to share is **that you need to verify the rental number's cleanliness before renting it long-term.** For example, I got two numbers from Nadanada; one can register for most apps I tested, but the other had trouble with one app.

Another issue I've found so far is that **once the rental period expires, you can't renew the same number anymore, and all your message history is gone too**, which isn't good if you want to use it for something important. You can definitely rent it for one year or longer and even set a remind email, but do keep that in mind.

*I have a suggestion: how about giving people a grace period to renew the same number after it expires? Maybe even an option to download the message history.* @nadanada_me

***

### **The Art of Slowly Exiting the Fiat World**

I'm aware that a local SIM is necessary for local delivery and any Gov-related things, but it's better to limit its use; for example, avoid using it to register any of your online profiles.

My current setup is a prepaid local SIM, Silent Link for internet, and Nadanada for sites that need a verification code. The best part about these Bitcoin e-SIMs is that you pay for what you actually use, and even better: **you might develop a better habit of using your phone less when you're out!**

Less screen time, less internet use, spend less money (save more sats), and spend more time in real life with people around you, which sounds quite a good deal! I've started taking a notebook with me now. Since I am learning a new language, I can spend more time learning instead of checking what's going on on the internet.

***

### **Disclosures**

I won't get paid or anything for recommending them, I just enjoy finding tools that make my life easier, and happy to share my experience. **After you try how things work with Bitcoin, you simply CAN'T go back to fiat companies.** Since a few people have asked previously, "Will you use Bitcoin as your everyday money?" It actually starts with small things like this.

Once you taste the simplicity and peace of mind compared with fiat companies, you will slowly try to find alternatives to exit the fiat world. Even better, you learn how to create it yourself if you can't find it.

Enjoy! ⚡️

items.title: Latest Strikes #36 & #37 - Augst 31st - September 13th 2026
items.text:
Welcome to Latest Strikes, your (lately bi-) weekly report of the latest Lightning-related news. As in the past few issues, this edition is heavily focused on software security releases. We've got releases from all major implementations to cover, exploits, and more.

![](https://m.stacker.news/157252)

## rust-lightning Release & Candidate

[https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.3-rc1](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.3-rc1) of [rust-lightning](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning) was released 2 weeks ago, improving on splicing, Bolt12 and more. A few personal picks:

* pending splices can now be RBF'd, and it is now possible to splice funds in and out in a single transaction;
* Bolt12 payments can now receive arbitrary metadata, and support for Bolt12 [Payer Proofs](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-21#experimental-bolt12-payer-proofs-in-core-lightning) was added;
* anchor channels can now drop the requirement for a remote (trusted) party to hold a reserve in the channel, which is especially useful in the LSP context as it allows the user to spend their whole balance.

Note that this release brings some incompatibilities. Notably:

* v0.3-rc1 is a breaking change for Bolt11 invoices carrying metadata, because now the invoice's secret commits to those. Existing metadata-bearing invoices will be invalidated, and invoices generated under v0.3-rc1 would be invalidated by a downgrade;
* outbound payments still awaiting a Bolt12 invoice response won't complete across the upgrade;
* Bolt12 refunds issued before the update will not be claimable after updating.

See the full [backwards compatibility report](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.3-rc1#user-content-backwards-compatibility) before upgrading.

A week later, the maintenance release [0.2.6](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.2.6) was also released, bringing bug and security fixes to the stable 0.2 line:

* a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4983) to a bug that could lead to a node crashing on restart in some circumstances. When a channel is closed while it has not seen any activity and doesn't hold any funds for the node, the node archives the monitoring of this channel right away, since there's nothing else to do about it. However, this early archiving could lead to a state where the `ChannelManager` component still holds an entry for this channel, but with no corresponding monitoring, leading to a crash on restart (the manager refuses to deserialize);
* a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4905) in rust-lightning's splice negotiation protocol, where a counterparty initiating a splice could inflate their apparent contribution to the fee[^1], passing checks while actually paying a lower fee than agreed. Crucially, this lowers the effective transaction fee, potentially increasing confirmation time, while letting the initiator pocket the difference in their own output;
* a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4982) to another bug where the `ChannelManager` refuses to deserialize on restart, this time caused by a bogus HTLC (immediately rejected but leaving an empty entry) followed by a valid and successfully forwarded HTLC with the same hash. This can be triggered remotely by anyone routing a payment through your node, and leads to the same failure on restart as the above "early channel archiving" bug.

Outside of these releases, a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4954) was also merged for a stale buffer bug that could lead to a channel force close after a splice, if the peers disconnect at a specific point during the splice protocol. This bug was found through fuzzing.

## Core Lightning Embargo Ending & Heads Up

There have been [reports](https://x.com/evankaloudis/status/2099582283409674260) early this week of users getting funds [stolen](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning/issues/9498) on (even the latest version of) Core Lightning when using the dual-funding feature. Yesterday, Core Lightning's official X account issued a [Security Advisory](https://x.com/Core_LN/status/2099927317107839188), urging operators to disable all [experimental features](https://docs.corelightning.org/reference/lightningd-config#experimental-options) immediately while investigations continue. Such experimental features include dual-funding, some LSP-related features, and more. While incredibly wide, this advice appears to confirm the substantiality of the above reports, so Core Lightning operators should exercise extreme caution. When possible, the `--offline` flag remains an [option](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-34-35#:~:text=Restart%20in%20%E2%80%9Coffline%E2%80%9D%20mode%2E) to stop peer traffic while still watching the chain.

On another note, the embargo on the latest Core Lightning [release](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-34-35#core-lightning-release) was lifted last Friday (September 11th), meaning we now have access to the source code for this [release](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning/releases/tag/v26.06.7). If you have not yet done so, I strongly encourage you to update to this latest version (v26.06.7) of Core Lightning.

An analysis of the [changelog](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning/compare/v26.06.6...v26.06.7) shows a few predominant topics. While the summary below is definitely not exhaustive, it covers some of the fixes that appear especially important to me.

### Revoked Commitment Disguised As Mutual Close (scaryyyy)

When a peer opens a channel with no upfront shutdown script, they can specify this script later, at close time. It was possible for an attacker to cause a Core Lightning node to mis-classify a force close with a revoked commitment as a mutual close, by using the `to_local` script of a past commitment as the shutdown script. Failing to detect the force close, the CLN node would not broadcast a justice transaction, allowing the peer to steal funds.

### On-chain Preimage vs. Unfinished Failure

Given 2 HTLCs with the same payment hash, a peer can fulfill one and fail the other, stop before either removal is final (old state revoked), and claim both HTLCs on-chain with the preimage. In that case, the specification adequately states that the preimage path wins, but Core Lightning would skip the "pending fail" HTLC. For a routing node, this could lead to loss of funds, since the outgoing HTLC is settled on-chain but the incoming one is never settled and eventually times out.

### On-chain Feerate Fixes

As we all know, Lightning remains strongly anchored to on-chain Bitcoin. While this is what confers Lightning its very strong self-custodial guarantees, it also comes with the drawback of exposing Lightning nodes to a range of bugs and attacks stemming from badly managed on-chain feerates.

* In mutual closes, a CLN node could apparently be "talked into" paying a higher feerate than it would have under a unilateral close. The unilateral close feerate, fed from the estimator with current on-chain conditions, now acts as an upper bound for the negotiation of the mutual close feerate;
* In splicing and dual-funding, a CLN node would accept any feerate from the peer, even if outside of the node's boundaries, which weren't properly piped there. A counterparty could therefore have the CLN node store an absurdly high feerate, or on the other side agree to a feerate as low as 0 (for dual-funding, splicing already has a lower bound), causing untimely confirmation or no valid RBF path. In the case of Core Lightning accepting absurdly high feerates in splicing/dual-funding, this could render RBF impossible (due to Bolt 2 ["25/24 rule"](https://github.com/lightning/bolts/blob/master/02-peer-protocol.md#rationale-5)), and could even in some cases lead to a node-wide crash loop on startup due to a u32 overflow.

### Remote DoS Fixes

Speaking of crashes, this security release also addresses a number of remotely triggerable DoS vectors, on top of the "feerate poisoning" one mentioned above.

* a node hostname crafted to be over 248 bytes, advertised through gossip, could crash the `connectd` subdaemon when attempting to connect to the corresponding node, crashing the whole node;
* a specifically crafted onion message could crash the offers plugin, resulting in a wider crash of the whole node;
* peers could have as many simultaneous dual-funded (v2) channel openings in progress as they wanted, which could exhaust a Core Lightning node's resources with a very high number of in-flight channel openings;
* an especially large unauthenticated request to a `clnrest` endpoint with a bad rune would crash the node with a segfault. This of course only affects nodes running clnrest, with the corresponding port open;
* some deeply nested JSON could exhaust the C stack and crash the process parsing the offending JSON. For example, `commando` parses peer-supplied JSON before checking the rune, so any connected peer could crash the plugin and the node.

## LND Release

Version [0.21.3](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/releases/tag/v0.21.3-beta) of LND is out, identical to the release candidate we covered [2 weeks ago](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-34-35#lnd-releases). On top of what we already covered there, notable changes are:

* the fix to a [bug](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/pull/10782) that could lead channels to end up in a limbo state if during a mutual close negotiation a peer disconnected before the close transaction was finalized;
* the [fix](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/pull/10869) to a bug where the channel counterparty spending an HTLC output could be treated as the node's own success transaction, passing a non-existent output to the sweeper, potentially poisoning sweep batches[^2];
* a new [RPC](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/pull/11065) enabling the creation of on-chain sub-wallets with spending capabilities inside the same node, allowing a single wallet to be split into smaller pockets that each control their own outputs. This new feature is experimental, and funds held in these sub-wallets cannot be recovered with only the seed phrase.

## Eclair Release

I'd like to mention *en passant* that ACINQ published a security [release](https://github.com/ACINQ/eclair/releases/tag/v0.14.3) for Eclair last Monday. Since this new version was released only 2 days ago, it belongs to next week's newsletter, but I wanted to let you know so you can update as soon as possible. Per ACINQ's release notes, the developers "highly recommend upgrading, as some of these issues can be exploited by malicious nodes".

## Electrum Release

Version [4.8.2](https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/blob/master/RELEASE-NOTES#:~:text=Release%204.8.2%20(September%2011%2C%202026)%20(security%20update)) of the Electrum wallet was released, and it's a security release. It includes several Lightning-related fixes, notably:

* payments sent are [no longer](https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/pull/10962) marked as failed when the receiver can still claim them because there are still some pending HTLCs;
* multiple fixes to payment forwarding, which is still experimental in Electrum;
* for some wallets (those using non-deterministic Lightning keys and anchor channels), the channel backup missed some critical key material, making recovery of funds in Lightning channels impossible because they lacked the key to sweep the `to_remote` output after the peer force-closed the channel. This is now [fixed](https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/pull/10852).

## Alby Hub Vulnerability For Old Versions

A [vulnerability](https://x.com/getAlby/status/2097574956049498150) affecting old versions (more than a year!) of Alby Hub appear to have been exploited in the wild. We don't have the full details yet, but it seems the vulnerability could "allow an attacker who could reach the Hub's management API to gain unauthorized access and send funds", if the Hub is publicly accessible from the internet.

Please, in the name of Satoshi, update your software, especially if it holds keys to Bitcoin funds. The affected versions here are v1.7.0 to v1.18.5 (prior to August 2025), and version 1.19.0 (August 2025) or newer are unaffected.

## Swiss Bitcoin Pay Vulnerability & Hack

While doing a generalized [review](https://kek.lol/research/appstore-wallets/) of Bitcoin wallets available on app stores, [BlueWallet](https://bluewallet.io/) CTO Igor (aka overtorment) found a critical vulnerability in [Swiss Bitcoin Pay](https://swiss-bitcoin-pay.ch/) (SBP), an app that lets merchants receive on-chain and Lightning payments without having to manage a node. On-chain payments are directly sent to the merchant's wallet in self-custody, and Lightning payments are sent to SBP's Lightning node and automatically withdrawn to the merchant's on-chain wallet periodically (e.g. every 24 hours). However, as Igor found, the app posted the full BIP39 mnemonic to its API when a user completed wallet signup/login. This has since been [fixed](https://github.com/SwissBitcoinPay/app/commit/1a23cb2e811f584639bdfe01d78765705bdc2398), but the extent to which user seeds were exposed remains unclear. If you used SBP before, it is strongly advised to remove funds from the wallet and create a new one.

Shortly after the finding, SBP's systems were also [breached](https://x.com/SwissBitcoinPay/status/2099473448162488618), potentially (personal opinion here!) by an actor looking to access the mnemonics if those were stored or logged on SBP's servers. According to SBP's communication, user funds are safe (which I believe includes Lightning funds that were pending automatic dispatch), and "any amounts owed to users will be fully returned". However, attackers "may have accessed customer email addresses, Bitcoin addresses and IBANs, transaction history, and hashed passwords" and it is "not yet clear whether any other information was accessed".

So yeah, this is pretty bad. Once again, if you have funds on an SBP wallet, I encourage you to move them to a new wallet asap.

## Zeus Release

Zeus [v13.2.1](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/releases/tag/v13.2.1) was released with, you guessed it, its load of security fixes. Especially worth noting are:

* the [bump](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4489) of the pinned LDK version used in Zeus (for the LDK embedded node) from a December 2025 snapshot to the 0.2 release branch head (v0.2.5). This therefore brings to Zeus all the LDK security fixes released up to v0.2.5 of rust-lightning;
* a [fix](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4362) to a bug (and potential vulnerability) whereby a user could review a given invoice A and end up paying a different invoice B when clicking "Pay". This could happen when a new invoice (B) was pushed to the wallet while the user had begun reviewing the first invoice (A). While the user initially reviewed invoice A, their validation would trigger the payment of invoice B. This second invoice could have been received in the wallet through any of the available vectors, including "the universal input router for QR, clipboard, deep links, and NFC";
* when paying an LNURL Pay URL or a Lightning Address, Zeus didn't check that the invoice's description hash matched the metadata supplied by the LNURL server, which could allow a malicious server to display "benign identity metadata" (e.g. what the Zeus user expects for this payment) while the actual invoice paid by the wallet "commits to an unrelated description hash \[or requests] an arbitrary amount". This is now [fixed](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4374).

## Zaprite

Zaprite [revealed](https://x.com/parkeralewis/status/2095534387844497702) the [Zaprite P2P App](https://zapritep2p.com/), with the goal of seamlessly coordinating payments between end users and across wallets. Reminiscent of Zaprite's main merchant payment facilitator [product](https://zaprite.com), users begin by connecting one or many of the supported wallets in the app. Someone wishing to pay them can then find them through the app (by username or phone number), pick which wallet they want to send from, and on the receiver's side Zaprite P2P will automatically route the payment to one of the connected wallets[^3]. Instead of the sender initiating the payment, the receiver can also create a payment request, where they can specify their preferred wallet for reception. If the sender doesn't have the app, a Zaprite P2P link allows them to pay nonetheless, directly to the receiver's wallet.

***

That's it for the last 2 weeks. As always, thank you so much for reading this far, and until next week!

[^1]: They achieve that by disguising the channel's current funding output as one of their own UTXOs added as input to the splicing transaction. The receiving node therefore treats the funds in the UTXO as belonging exclusively to the attacker, whereas they're actually shared funds in the channel.

[^2]: Because the underlying Bitcoin node rejects the sweep as invalid, since it tries to spend a non-existent output.

[^3]: There are many ways to handle this, but I guess an algorithm trying to minimize costs and maximize reliability will try to match the sender's wallet if the receiver also has it; and otherwise select the best next wallet on the receiver's side.

items.title: Using Bitcoin Miners to Make Maple Syrup
items.text:
Immersion mining with canola oil to concentrate maple sap more quickly
![](https://v.nostr.build/n997.mp4)
I'm using a single S9 hash board immersed in canola oil to heat maple sap to increase the effectiveness of the reverse osmosis sap concentration system.
![](https://i.nostr.build/okkw.jpg)
The weather conditions this season have caused the maple sap to be cold and stay cold which drastically slows down the ability of the RO system to filter water out of it. I ran into a bottle neck where there is more sap than I can keep up with concentrating so I needed to come up with something quickly!
![](https://i.nostr.build/B33D.jpg)
Ideally if the temperature of the sap is 77°f the filter will operate most effectively without damaging the RO membrane. Of course, my mind immediately turned to Bitcoin mining for the heating solution. What I came up with was an immersion system using the homebrew equipment I already had to heat the sap just before it entered the RO. This would allow the majority of the sap to stay cool keeping it from spoiling and still remove the most water possible.
![](https://i.nostr.build/e0Jz.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/aokZ.jpg)
The only thing I didn't have for the immersion system was the dielectric fluid. I had no idea where to find the proper fluid nor did it make sense to pay the high cost for it. The application for this system is very specific and I will only need it until April. I had been joking about using canola oil as dielectric fluid for almost a year but for this situation it seemed like the perfect fit. Canola oil is 70% cheaper than bitcool before shipping and was immediately available!
![](https://i.nostr.build/rDv2.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/J3qq.jpg)
Amazingly, I put everything together and it worked very well without major adjustments. I tip-toed the voltage and frequency of the single S9 hashboard up slowly to find the right balance in temperatures between the two fluid loops. Ultimately, I ended up with an overclocked board drawing over 600w! By the time I got the system setup and dialed in I was already half way through concentrating this collection of sap. The next collection will offer more concrete data on what this system is capable of. For now, even with the worst S9 board I have, I'm getting a 15% rebate on the total power usage of the whole process and it's definitely concentrating sap more quickly. All for ~$10 of canola oil... 👀

items.title: Trip Report: Paris
items.text:
Paris is known for its food and savoir vivre, the art of living your life. It comes as no surprise that the merchants I found accepting Bitcoin in Paris are all serving foods and drinks, and so this trip report is almost more of a food review than a Bitcoin review.

🧆In the hip 18th arrondissement lies Chez Ginette, a fairly typical cafe with its seats facing the trottoir, so Parisians can watch each other. The menu offers all the classic dishes you would expect from a place like this, but somehow lacks a theme or specialization. I order the greatest classic there is, the steak tartare. It comes préparé, meaning the raw egg is mixed in. It's definitely of high quality and I'm also happy about the pommes frites on the side. There is a "Bitcoin Lightning payments accepted" sticker on the door, and as I ask to pay with Bitcoin the waiter does not hesitate, although it takes him a while to get his colleague to come over with an orange point of sale terminal running the Swiss Bitcoin Pay app, built on BTCPay. The payment goes through almost instantly.

🍸Le Greffulhe is another cafe close to the opera and a high-end fashion district. As I arrive I mistake a man standing by the entrance for staff and ask him about Bitcoin paymnets. He says he would be surprised if they did, and indeed he is after we go inside together to ask the cashier. The cafe belongs to the same category as Chez Ginette, but the atmosphere feels very different, and although they do serve food, I never got the chance to try it during my two visits. Instead I had Aperol Spritz and Campari Soda, and payments went smoothly to the mobile phone of the cashier, also running Swiss Bitcoin Pay.

🍺Undoubtedly the heart of the Paris Bitcoin community is N'importe Quoi near Les Halles, somewhat in the geographical center of the city. The dive bar has the kind of anarchic and old-school feminist feel of a place that you almost expect to be taking Bitcoin. I'm here quite early and all by myself, and at first the bar tender denies my Bitcoin payment, saying "usually we do." Eventually she shows mercy with me and digs up the phone that has fallen somewhere behind the cash register, presumably only kept for the sole purpose of processing Bitcoin payments. The bar also uses Swiss Bitcoin Pay, and I'm quite pleased with how fast I can find a route to their node, and how I never paid more than 0.09% in fees, just a few sats.

🍝The Italian restaurant Costa d'Amalfi greets visitors with a warning: No Pizza. Connoisseurs will recognize this as a sign of quality, and indeed the family-run trattoria is exactly the kind of place you typically see accepting Bitcoin in Italy. Everything is well curated, the menu is short and specializes in one thing: truffle dishes. The owner comes over to talk to me about Bitcoin, telling me stories of his family and his Bitcoin story. He also uses the now familiar Swiss Bitcoin Pay and is quite happy with it.

🥮Located near Volontaires, an hommage to the volunteer soldiers of the French Revolution, is one of the areas of Paris known for their contemporary bohème lifestyle. Le Drapeau de la Fidélité fits it perfectly with its nondescript facade and carefully curated interior. There are plenty of books that make the restaurant feel more like a library, and they appear to have actually been read frequently. There are antiques, paintings, signed letters and a banner proclaiming a "Universal Humanist Capitalist Society" that I cannot find any other information about. The owner, a well-dressed older Vietnamese gentleman appears to run the tiny restaurant with its maybe 12 seats together with his son. The menu is short and the dishes simple and affordable. I order the porc caramélisé and pay a round 18,000 satoshi. The owner seems quite pleased with me paying with Bitcoin, which is always a great feeling when spending it. He uses Cake wallet, but doesn't know how to set an amount for his invoices. Also, his wallet is priced in USD, meaning I have to look up the rate on my end. As far as routing fees go, it's by far my most expensive payment at 0.3%.

🍷Near the Gare d'Austerlitz I visit La Brasserie L'Audièrnes. The area seems to be very popular with students, and everyone at the bar seems to be talking about AI, with many conversations in English. I order my drink at the bar and pay right away, but the cashier is hesitant to show me his wallet, and instead asks his colleague over. We navigate through the interface of some unfamiliar crypto wallet, and all we can find is an onchain address, which I pay to reluctantly.

I'm quite happy with my visit to Paris and especially the Bitcoin places that I found. I love the opportunity to find some random or hidden gems in the city that I would have never been able to visit if it weren't for Bitcoin. I love talking to the staff and the owners, there is always something to learn, and sometimes to teach, about how people are using Bitcoin. I also went to six other places, four of which were closed, and two of which no longer accept Bitcoin. At one of these places, the doors and cash register covered in Bitcoin stickers, I was practically laughed at for asking to pay with Bitcoin, before being asked to pay one Bitcoin to buy everyone a round. Finally one reason to implement BIP 177.

items.title: Pregnant Thoughts at 25 weeks
items.text:
Well, there's no doubt about the baby growing in my belly, he/she makes their presence known at least once, sometimes twice a day. Little nudges, little fits of movement against my skin. How quickly I have found reassurance and connection in that teeny, fluttery feeling. Plus, if you looked at me, you'd see the bump. I fit into less than half of my wardrobe. It's fun to grow, it's fun to see the changes. Even watching the number on my scale go up and up, it's confirmation. I waited a long while for this experience to be real, and I'm just relishing in its reality.

I characterized my pregnancy as *mild* when I wrote about [the first trimester](https://stacker.news/items/1513553). I would still use that language today, maybe I'd say it's been easy, compared to what I hear it can be. My body is making all kinds of adjustments as it regulates the work of growing one and maintaining another, but I'm pretty blissfully unaware of its efforts. During the first trimester, there was one day I was sick, some mothers are sick for the entirety of that period. And during this one, I've had one evening of heartburn, when some mothers also experience this throughout. I'm thankful for that!

# Baby's birth medicalized

The biggest challenge has been a mental one. We've risked out of midwife care and will be transferring all scans and plans from here to inside the hospital with obstetricians. Pretty big bummer for me, I've never been a hospital patient and I don't anticipate I'll make a very good one. Having been propaganized against hospital birth since college, I had pretty strong avoidance and resistance feelings to get through once it became evident that baby may be outside the normal standards that midwives practice in. But I'm also a person of faith and trust in God whose will is better than my desires. The news that I'll have to transfer is pretty new, but in the short span of a few days, I have come to an acceptance that must be supernaturally inspired. I've seen evidence of a plan that's better than my own, orchestrated in spite of me, for the good of me and my tiny one. Clinging to resistance doesn't make the going any easier, and in my determination not to operate from fear, I choose acceptance.

The specific diagnosis is Intrauterine Growth Restriction, IUGR or FGR sometimes. What it means is my baby is smaller than the average of all babies for its gestational age. And baby has been small throughout the entirety of my pregnancy, it was noted at my first 8 week scan. The encouraging thing is that baby continues to grow along a positive curve, but being below 10% of the average is a disqualifying factor for a birth supported by midwives, without medical attention/intervention. Because it was introduced early on, I have been able to steep myself in whatever rich information I can find about this issue (I was building a case to fight it off, but this is not that kind of problem to solve; I rest my case). I'm reading anecdotes from message boards, listening to podcasts, taking in any input about growth restriction and birth outcomes. If you have any relevant experience or know anyone who does, I'll be happy to hear about it.

I'd also be interested in any book recommendations. After *Guide to Childbirth*, I don't really have anything else on the list.

Learning this lesson early in my child's life, that my best mode of operation is to be flexible/adaptable rather than rigid/stubborn in the face of change, is probably the best parent primer. Do you agree?

items.title: Swing and a miss: Paying with Bitcoin on a Square Terminal
items.text:
This year, I've got my kids doing a homeschool co-op two days a week. This just means that a group of homeschool parents have organized to teach their children in a group setting, and possibly hire a teacher or two for subjects where more formal education might be helpful (languages, music, science?). 

Unfortunately, the coop we have joined is quite some way from our home, so after dropping off the children, I go to a nearby coffee shop to work -- a coffee shop that has a Square terminal.

I have asked if they accept Bitcoin a number of times so far, but in all cases the cashier's answer has been "I don't think so" or "I'll have to talk to the person who manages this" (pointing at the terminal). It's a busy place and so there is often a line, and I haven't wanted to try to make anyone wait while I help figure out how to turn on Bitcoin payments, and so I haven't made much progress. 

Today, the person behind the cash register was the owner and I seized my opportunity. 

I placed my order and while he was ringing it up, I said, "I've heard that these Square terminals accept bitcoin."

The owner glanced up at me and said, "I've heard that, too. Let's see if we can figure it out."

This was a much more enthusiastic response than I was expecting. He poked away at the terminal for a few minutes and then said, "I think it only takes bitcoin if you have CashApp."

I told him that this was not the case, but that if he could get it to display a QR code I could try paying that.

He continued to tap on the terminal without much effect. I should say this terminal was not the sort that has a rotatable screen. There is one fixed screen facing the cashier and a smaller fixed screen facing the customer. This was showing the message "Waiting for cashier..."

"I think you have to tap to pay," he said.

Now, I don't use any of the Lightning wallets that have implemented tap to pay (as far as I remember there aren't very many) so that wasn't an option. I told him that I needed a QR code to scan.

After another couple minutes, the owner volunteered: "Maybe I can text it to you." 

I am usually loathe to provide a phone number, but in the interest of dismantling the legacy financial system, I gave it to him. I immediately received a text with a link. The link was to pay for my coffee, but had required fields for name, phone number, and email. At the bottom I saw a green button that said pay with CashApp or something like that. I tapped it, but nothing happened because I had not entered the required fields. 

Still in the interest of taking down the fiat empire, I entered some incorrect information in these fields. But then when I tapped the green button, it presented me with a message informing me that I did not have CashApp and a button to download CashApp. 

At this point the line behind me was long enough that I offered to pay with cash and the owner accept with some visible signs of relief.

So: I have failed on this the fourth time I've tried to pay with Bitcoin at this Square terminal. I suspect that the owner needs to turn Bitcoin payments on and that I will need to talk him through this process, so I'll have to rewatch those videos about how to do this. 

It occurs to me that Square could do a lot better with this flow if they had a button that allowed the cashier to display a QR code that was simultaneously a CashApp code and a Lightning invoice. This is a lot to ask, but I'm pretty sure it needs to be at least that easy for it to work well.

items.title: Guilty until proven innocent
items.text:
ALL surveillance and control, all AML, KYC and all violations of privacy are completely unethical, immoral and illegitimate. All of them! As recently as the 1990s, one could purchase stocks without providing identification. Bank deposits below arbitrary thresholds required no explanation or documentation. Cash transactions, regardless of size, were presumed legitimate unless specific evidence suggested otherwise. The default assumption was that individuals had the right to conduct their financial affairs privately, with the burden of proof resting on authorities to demonstrate wrongdoing before intruding upon that privacy.

This historical norm was not an oversight or a failure of governance, it was a recognition of a fundamental principle. Free societies operate on the presumption of innocence, treating citizens as autonomous agents capable of managing their own affairs unless proven otherwise through due process. The current system inverts this relationship entirely, treating every citizen as a potential criminal whose financial activities must be continuously monitored and pre-approved by state bureaucrats. Given how KYC for everything short of going to a rest room is being normalized, the world needs more privacy protecting tools, not less.

items.title: Is L-BTC a shitcoin?
items.text:
# The closest I've ever come to being a shitcoiner

Back in 2024, I spent a lot of time looking at ecash. Ecash is cool -- it has all these neat properties like potentially better privacy and maybe being a bearer asset like cash and being so lightweight that almost anyone can run a mint and cypherpunks have been working on ecash since long before bitcoin. Development in Cashu and Fedimint was in full flower and there weren't many viable alternatives like Ark or Spark.

@TonyGiorgio wrote a post in January of 2024 called "Fedimint is Self-Custodial" https://stacker.news/items/395461 which was the catalyst for a particular fascination of mine: trying to determine what sort of thing an ecash token actually is. Is it like a gift card? https://stacker.news/items/397764/r/Scoresby or a repurchase agreement a la the Fed's repo window? https://stacker.news/items/565172/r/Scoresby Is it a token you buy? https://stacker.news/items/554143/r/Scoresby

It was clear to me that ecash tokens were not bitcoin, but at that point in Bitcoin culture if a token wasn't bitcoin, it could only be a shitcoin -- and yet I didn't think using ecash was shitcoining. I think this was because I associate shitcoining with scamming and degenerate trading and pump 'n dump schemes while ecash was clearly trying to do payments.

I got so interested in the idea that I believe @Car felt compelled to block me and I recall a number of fiery conversations with @justin_shocknet.

# Justin was right

There were many points about which we disagreed, but I believe one of the most significant was that I tried to defend the use of ecash as less trusting than simply relying on a custodian. About this, I was most certainly wrong. Here is Justin [explaining it to me](https://stacker.news/items/554143/r/Scoresby?commentId=554230):

![](https://m.stacker.news/155829)

# Why the change of mind

That last bit in Justin's comment gets at it. I wanted to think about a mint in isolation or as a complete system, but this is obviously not the case. Ecash mints are an attempt to glue a non-bitcoin system onto bitcoin and so evaluating as some whole thing on its own was not particularly relevant to users who were interested in sats.

This was made painfully clear by the recent Liquid hack. There are 15 "geographically distributed" Liquid functionaries in their federation and at least 11 of them are required to finalize blocks. And yet, almost the entire amount of bitcoin in the Liquid Network was withdrawn and block production was halted.

In that moment, calling a Liquid wallet self-custodial was pretty clearly demonstrated to be wrong. If you have a L-BTC balance in ACQUA Wallet, Manna Wallet, or Misty Breez you can't move your sats (and you may not actually have any sats). Doesn't sound very self-custodial.

This interaction with @Roy_Breez was very enlightening:

![](https://imgprxy.stacker.news/Uv9piRjMpEGZXhf394gOtE-JsUrOj3DSE49enKKft_8/rs:fit:2560:1440/aHR0cHM6Ly9tLnN0YWNrZXIubmV3cy8xNTU3ODU)

![](https://imgprxy.stacker.news/Nen5MnjrhiSPdtgEtJxk1bsSkcl-edx0-smACu0JfwQ/rs:fit:2560:1440/aHR0cHM6Ly9tLnN0YWNrZXIubmV3cy8xNTU3ODY)

We've been calling these things self-custodial, but the users can't use their money and possibly don't even have it any more.

# Okay, but Coldcard users also lost funds out of their wallets...

This may seem like a pedantic point, but it really drove it home for me. The key difference between Coldcard users and Liquid users that makes one self-custodial and the other custodial is that when you open a Liquid-based wallet right now, it still shows your balance...you just don't have it. Both Coldcard users and Liquid users have experienced theft -- but the latter still have their L-BTC and that makes all the difference. Because what value does L-BTC have if there's no BTC in the Liquid Federation wallet? (or even if there's not enough BTC there?)

I wanted to be able to call things like ecash tokens and L-BTC something other than a shitcoin because I thought there was a way for them to be used in lieu of bitcoin, but the reality is that such an approach muddies the water. If we are going to call a bitcoin wallet self-custodial, the bitcoin wallet shouldn't show you a balance when there isn't one.[^1]

# Where does this leave me and my fascination with ecash and other fake L2s?

I don't think L-BTC is a shitcoin. But it ***is*** more accurate to call Liquid *custodial*. Same goes for ecash, Ark, Spark, and all the other fake L2s.

[^1]: And for you jerks who will observe that a bitcoin node that is not yet updated could also display a balance that isn't there, go look at Bitcoin Core: they have a pretty big warning that says your balance may not be accurate when you aren't synced to the current chaintip.

items.title: How life gets in the way of Stacker News
items.text:
I’ve been largely offline and not really on SN much these days. Mostly a collection of small things, like health issues that aren’t in the “oh shit” realm, but which take up lots of time and energy (neither my wife nor I have figured out how to stop getting older - other than the one obvious one - and that means more health bullshit each day, apparently). Plus work just being, well, work. And assorted miscellaneous things. Much as I love SN, I only have so much time in a given day.

But this in turn has made it clear how much I need a better subscription page for SN. When I do have time for SN, I hit my subscription page and it’s fucking overwhelming. If I’m lucky, I can see maybe twelve hours worth of stuff, but sometimes, it’s only a few hours.

I subscribe to maybe eight territories, and maybe as many individual posters. But that’s enough (especially as some of the territories have gotten busier) to completely overwhelm my feed. I’ve missed plenty of important posts ([one costing me 10K sats](https://stacker.news/items/1571441) [^1]), and plenty more where I’d have loved to contributed to discussions.

One obvious solution would be to just reduce what I subscribe to. But that’s self-defeating. I subscribe to people and communities because I like them and want updates. I also (obviously) want notifications on posts I make and when I’m tagged.

What I’d like (and I have no idea if this is on the radar, nor if it’s easy/possible) is the ability to break up my subscription page. The aggregate page is fine when I’m on a lot. But when I’m not, allow me to see territory subscriptions from separately from the user subscriptions separately from the comments on my actual posts. I could manually just change all my settings each time, but if I had the time to do all that all the time, I’d have the time to keep up with my feeds. As it stands, having a lack of time to keep up with SN is, in itself, something that causes me to fall behind even further on SN.

I'm always reluctant to request features/changes that may only help me, but putting this out there as something that others who are short on time (assuming I'm not the only person whose entire life doesn't revolve around SN) might also want to weigh in on?

[^1]: Not really, since I’d have lost eventually, and probably soon. But I can keep telling myself that's not true.

House Set To Take First Step To Establish A Federal Strategic Bitcoin Reserve
items.text:
Tomorrow at 10:00 am the House Financial Services Committee is set to consider [H.R. 8957](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8957/text), the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026. This bill was introduced back in May by Republican Rep. Nick Begich of Alaska, and the legislations lead cosponsor is Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, making it a bipartisan bill. 

Under this legislation, the Treasury Secretary would establish two separate structures. First, within 180 days of signing into law, the Treasury Secretary would establish a secure storage facility, the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. Second, a separate "Digital Assets Stockpile" would be established to handle all other crypto besides Bitcoin held by the Federal Government. The Treasury Secretary would have discretion to sell, exchange, or convert non-Bitcoin crypto, and the proceeds of this are required to be used to increase the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve ***OR*** reduce the National Debt.  

Since this is legislation, naturally Bitcoin had to be defined. Called "qualifying Bitcoin," this is BTC finally forfeited through criminal or civil asset forfeiture proceedings, or received in satisfaction of certain civil monetary penalties subject to requirements under existing Federal law. 

The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve is subject to a long holding period as well. Bitcoin the government currently has would have to remain in the reserve for at least 20 years from when the reserve was created. Bitcoin added after the fact would also face a 20-year lock-up where it could not be sold, swapped, auctioned, etc. Two years before the minimum holding period (18 years after creation), the Treasury Secretary is required to provide a report to Congress with recommendations on whether the Government should continue holding its Bitcoin or permit a gradual release. At the 20-year mark, the Sec. could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve during any two-year period. This limits any sort of release that the Administration at the time would want to perform. 

In a move to keep the Government's BTC holdings public, the Treasury would also be required to establish a public-facing, ongoing proof-of-reserve system, disclose holdings and transactions, and have these reports reviewed by an independent third-party auditor.

The legislation also touches on a variety of other things, like budget-neutral BTC purchases, states being able to put their BTC holdings in segregated accounts within the reserve, protecting private ownership by stating that this bill cannot be used to authorize federal seizure or confiscation of lawfully acquired Bitcoin, and more.

items.title: How do you teach your children to defend themselves?
items.text:
In my view, teaching our children to defend themselves is vital to their upbringing.

Defending yourself means more than just landing a good blow; it also encompasses knowing how to respond confidently, how to ask for help, and how to recognize when walking away is the best option.

I am going to focus on the school environment the place where our children find themselves without our supervision and care. In my view, this is where they put into practice everything they have learned at home, since that is where their social interactions originate.

At home, we have taught our daughter to follow three  steps in case someone bothers her verbally: First, ignore it; if that doesn't work, respond in a firm voice; third, ask a teacher for help.

Defending herself against physical attacks: Since she doesn't know how to fight, I tell her she should run away and ask for help immediately. I haven't told her things like "hit back," "push," or similar things because she won't do it the right way. She's small and thin, and it could all end up being worse if she tries to defend herself against physical attacks on her own. She did karate for a while, but the truth is she didn't like it and didn't learn much. This year I want to enroll her in kickboxing classes. I don't want her to be a bully, I don't want her to be the one to throw the first punch, I don't want her to be the one looking for trouble, but I do want her to know how to throw the right punch or subdue the person who tries to attack her.

Sadly, she has reached the age where she could encounter a peer who might want to sexually assault her ranging from stealing a kiss or groping her to something far more serious. I only pray that life is kind to her and spares her from such horrific experiences; still, my job as a mom is to make things clear so she knows how to recognize when she is being assaulted.

I tell her that asking an adult for help won't make her a coward; on the contrary, it shows intelligence.

The new school year is about to start in Venezuela, and I’m a little nervous, praying that the days go well.

You are valuable; your voice is important and deserves to be heard. No one is superior to you, and you are not superior to anyone else. These are the phrases I constantly repeat to her.

items.title: Another bitcoin adoption story
items.text:
Lately, I haven’t been able to find time for meetups because of family and work, so I decided to focus on lunches instead. In a regular local pub, I asked the owner if he’d be willing to accept Bitcoin. He politely declined.

I kept going there about once a week. After a few visits, I made an NFC card and loaded it with 1,000 sats as a tip. I also gave him a leaflet with instructions on how to access the Bitcoin. He’s an older gentleman, not very interested in technology, and doesn’t have much time for experiments while running the place. The following week, I tipped him another 1,000 sats. On the third week, he finally agreed to let me install a mobile wallet app for him.

Suddenly, he had a bit of Bitcoin in his Wallet of Satoshi. I asked him if I could start paying that way — with the promise that if it didn’t work out, I’d exchange it back into cash for him. He wasn’t too keen at first, but since I was a regular, he wanted to make me happy.

From that moment, I announced in the local Jednadvacet (our Czech version of Einundzwanzig) community that we’d meet for lunch every Thursday. A short meetup — a chance to exchange Bitcoin, learn something new, meet people, etc. The only condition: payment must be in Bitcoin.

Two months have passed since then. The group has been growing. At first, there were just three of us. Last time, there were already seventeen. For the owner, it’s become a significant part of that day’s revenue. He’s started treating us better too — now he greets us from afar and even reserves the biggest table for us every Thursday, not letting anyone else sit there.

Every time I ask him if everything’s okay, if he wants to cash out, or needs any help with it. And you know what he told me last time? That he doesn’t need to — it’s growing nicely in Bitcoin. He even recently bought a fridge with Bitcoin. He said he had to use Lightning because he ran into some issues with on-chain. I never even mentioned the word “Lightning” to him. He’s been learning on his own, and now he’s become quite the Bitcoiner.

It looks like the pub might soon turn into a nice little vexl point — a place where people can exchange Bitcoin for dirty fiat and vice versa.

I’m writing this because I think it’s a great blueprint. It’s short, takes me about an hour a week — time I’d spend on lunch anyway — I meet people, and it helps Bitcoin adoption in a very natural way. Hopefully, it’ll inspire more Bitcoiners to try something similar in their own area.

The chicken coop was battered by falling tree tops from recent heavy winds but the chicken compost system is still churning out compost and eggs.

![](https://i.nostr.build/Bl2VhTfRzigPZBS3.jpg)
The 40ish birds are working 4 compost piles every day, breaking them down and consuming as many worms and fly larvae as the can find.
![](https://i.nostr.build/iNdM1gBA4b9vO85C.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/1FYWKfVTojZYynTg.jpg)
Each day I spend 20 minutes rebuilding the piles and watering them with nutrient rich water from the duck bath. Then I spend 20 minutes collecting as much fresh horse manure as I can, adding it to the system. With each rebuilding of the piles, they march slowly forward from the back of the paddock to the front. By the time the pile reaches the front the compost is finished and ready for use around the homestead. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/MbGXG22ZdoocGVU6.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/jh60ABOg7vAYpU2V.jpg)
While I do some work to maintain the energy flow through the system, the chickens are doing good work on the piles, consuming horse fly larvae reducing the pest pressure on the horses, and paying me in eggs for the work. Meanwhile I'm feeding them less and less grain. We are producing yeilds beyond what we can utilize at the homestead so I've been selling the compost and eggs at Bitcoin meetups in my area. Distributing natural capital and strengthening my local Bitcoin culture and community. A great example of a permaculture system here at the homestead!


Our chickens system is inspired by Karl Hammer, Perma Pastures, and Edible Acres

items.title: Research in Public #20: Stacker News paper accepted at WISE 2026
items.text:
Almost exactly one year ago, I proposed to do a research paper using Stacker News data (https://stacker.news/items/1243188) and to do so in public, with all the code available in a public [github repo](https://github.com/ed-kung/sn-research), and regular public updates on the [progress of the research](https://stacker.news/SimpleStacker#research-in-public).

The first set of results were finished in around December 2025, and since then I've been trying to get it accepted at conferences and journals.  Unfortunately, the track record was not great.  A Bitcoin research conference did not take it (no reason given), the *Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization* did not take it (too niche), and *Electronics Commerce Research and Applications* did not take it (I don't write like an IS scholar).

But, I'm pleased to say that finally we are having some success. The paper was just accepted to the *Workshop on Information Systems and Economics*, which will be held in Lisbon, Portugal this December.  This is one of the main conferences for economists studying information systems, and the [program](https://wiseconf2026.github.io/) looks super interesting.  I think this is the right group of people to try and get this work in front of, and I'm looking forward to the feedback I get -- as well as the exposure Stacker News may receive from other researchers.

If you're interested, you can read a working draft of the paper [here](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6556022)

items.title: Bank Runs are Good, Actually: Death to the Central Banks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
ASTONISHING piece to see in regular financial press. *Maybe the tide is turning and the world is healing?*

![](https://m.stacker.news/159395)

The basic/most fundamental rationale for a central bank isn't financing the gov deficit (which they don't...*ish*) or set centralized interest rates, but to support commercial banks when faced with bank runs (=stand ready to lend against their assets, even if distressed, with newly created base money, so stave off the run.) The idea, from Francis Barings to Diamond\&Dybvig's [Nobel Prize](https://stacker.news/items/1583458?commentId=1583534) winning article, is that depositors are fickle and might/will run on perfectly healthy banks *and* that such runs cause real damage to the economy (*and* might spread through the banking system like wildfire and we all collapse into Great Depression 2.0).
*That's everything that's wrong with monetary economics and politics around central banks in one sentence...*

***

The authors of the paper Nangle discusses here used the Chronicling America project, scanned newspapers, then...

> they used LLMs to sift these articles further to find pieces about actual bank runs rather than, say, stuff about boats running into river banks, or the local bank manager running for mayor, and to match each report to individual banks.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159396)

> According to Verner, the research reveals that the idea that runs kill solvent banks is dramatically overstated. It turns out that depositors are actually pretty good at working out how dodgy a bank is, generally making runs on banks that are insolvent or very close to insolvent.

This is incredible. Specifically, — and I'm sparing you a deep dive into debates in financial history and monetary economics here — a big rationale for *why central banks must exist* is **to prevent bad types of bank runs.**

Running a bank means it has to shed assets, assets that aren't "finished," or turned into workable projects and thus liqudity, yet. (That's sort of the purpuse of a bank: to *liquify* illiquid assets, hold the maturity and duration mismatch in the meantime.)  Selling these assets quickly means taking (large) haircuts on book value, meaning a random run on a healthy bank can destroy projects or at least turn the bank itself bankrupt -- destroying customer relatioships and disrupting the bank-money-level money supply etc etc. 
**That's all unnecessary, and a benevolent central bank/observer can improve upon the state of the world by injecting more money and support the healthy bank.**

## ...except, depositors don't run on healthy banks!

That's what this beautiful history and database shows. Somehow, depositors (in aggregate) are clever enough to sniff out when something is wrong *and not* structurally/mindlessly/sunspot-style make erratic and concentrated mistakes.

If you scratch [the lender or last resort literature a little](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/when-did-the-bank-of-england-become-a-lender-of-last-resort/), you find that it's a good, disciplining market mechanism for depositors to run on banks. Here's a schematic:

* if bank is healthy and other bankers know it, then the bank can source enough liquidity from them ("recycling" deposits), against a very minimal short-term expense. **No problem, no negative outcome, no need for lender of last resort** 
* if the bank is unhealthy and the other bankers know it, they won't lend to it and it will fail, *and it will be a good thing!* Bankers taking bad risks or making bad investments should fail, like every other business in a market economy.
* if the bank is healthy, but the **other bankers don't know it** *and so refuse to lend*, that's when a lender of last resort needs to step in and save the day. By supplying that extra liquidity it can stave off the damaging run and everyone is better off for it.

Here's the best short article/overview I've ever seen on this (by [George Kaufman, for econlib](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/BankRuns.html)):

![](https://m.stacker.news/159394)

---

The literature on bank runs and central banks is basically an exercise in showing **whether or not the central bank knows about the true state of a given bank better than other bankers do.**

When central banks *also* had prudential obligation, by chance some of its workers would have recently audited and inspected private information for that bank, meaning it's quite plausible that central bankers *do* have some insider information here that they can act on. (Nowadays that function is usually separated to another agency, thus the argument is practically quite moot.)

But... If historically and practically depositors are good enough in aggregate to sniff out what's wrong, there's no *need* for a central bank to intervene and override their market choice.

Bank runs are bad for local economies

> ...only if the banks that are being abandoned have been making bad loans, a big borrower defaults, or something like that.

...in which case there is **a real economic loss that we want/need someone to carry** — not paper over and pretend it's not there. (\_cough\_, Bitfinex...)

***

Told yah:

> Surely **the mere process of a run on a healthy bank wreaked havoc on their local economy?** Apparently not.

> Cross-referencing each bank’s financial strength, the researchers trace the local economic impact of each bank run using Bradstreet’s contemporary reporting. They find that a run on a strong bank doesn’t really impose any economic cost at all on the local economy. Yet runs on banks whose fundamentals are awful are followed by major lending contractions that can cause all sorts of spillover problems.

and:

> Out of **3,984 bank runs on individual US banks from 1863–1934**, the authors identify 53 that look like they’re based on “misinformation” or “depositor confusion”, which reads as academese for “blind panic”. Of these 53 oddities, six banks failed, which sounds like maybe six too many. But the researchers argue that the historical data indicates that “strong banks (fundamentals in the upper tercile) subject to **non-fundamental runs have a zero probability of failure”**
> one of the footnotes indicates that at least one of these failed banks had basically committed massive fraud, which was only uncovered by their so-called irrational run.

*Even that*, the depositors sniffed out. Amazing.

***

All "pretty interesting" says Nangle, understating the explosive result.

> the ideas that the Nobel winners formalise are really the ones sitting behind the rationale for bank deposit insurance.

Yes. This evidence shows/weighs heavy that lender of last resort is a defunct and unnecessary function — liable to abuse, nepotism, and trigger-happy rulers, not actually saving a banking system that needs it

## Runs are good. Banks should fail more. And lender of last resort is an unnecessary function

items.title: How Private Are Bitcoin Transactions, Really? - Vinteum
items.text:
This is a pretty lengthy post, which has some echoes of slop, but which was also a nice survey of privacy in onchain bitcoin. The post is based on a five-day privacy focused retreat the Vinteum folks did. 

The post does a nice job of covering some of the concerns of onchain bitcoin, including chain analysis, wallet finger printing, and the asymmetrical nature of privacy: privacy must be constantly preserved, but one leak or mistake can have permanent consequences.

They cover payjoins and coinjoins and coinswaps and do a nice job of pointing out the strengths and weaknesses.

One particularly interesting note is that they mention something called the [Fungi Protocol](https://fungi-protocol.github.io/docs/) which looks to be a privacy project that Vinteum is working on. So far, the publicly available parts aren't very fleshed out, but it looks like they have a wallet-fingerprinting-blocker PSBT under development as well as some sort of collaborative spending technique. 

I'm curious to see what they make of Fungi. Definitely something to keep watching.

items.title: Nonrenewable Resources Never Truly Run Out (Mises Institute, JB)
items.text:
Recycling this beauty from 2019 for a very specific reason... I suppose ya'll will find out in a day or two

![](https://m.stacker.news/159301)

...as if I wasn't already on a mission to have the wokies and greenies *hate* my guts (https://stacker.news/items/1583743, https://stacker.news/items/1583533).

## Actually, "Renewable" is Bullshit and nonrenewable stuff never runs out

Here's the logic:

> In 1944 the world’s amount of proven oil reserves were 51bn barrels of oil. In 2018 the world’s proven oil reserves were almost 1,500bn (BP estimates [1,730](https://www.bp.com/en/global/corporate/energy-economics/statistical-review-of-world-energy/oil.html#oil-reserves)b[n ](https://www.bp.com/en/global/corporate/energy-economics/statistical-review-of-world-energy/oil.html#oil-reserves)), i.e., about thirty times that of 1944 — and this despite humanity’s pretty voracious appetite for oil during the seven-odd decades in between. Anyone immersed in the naïve resource depletion theory has to incredulously ask himself — *how can this be*?

> Simply put: we found more of it.

HOW?!

> In a trivial sense this is of course true: the anti-capitalist [environmentalists ](https://capx.co/the-totalitarianism-of-the-environmentalists/)are superficially correct about no [Planet B ](https://www.ecowatch.com/there-is-no-planet-b-1881704065.html)and the [impossibility of infinite growth of material consumption](https://www.brainyquote.com/quotes/e_f_schumacher_389554). But it’s also, as [Tim Worstall ](https://www.adamsmith.org/store/bzdlbo6oy071wbbz4v7fjgvoelr0ey)explains, **“supremely unimportant.”** In comparing the use of finite resources to food in the fridge, Worstall explodes the “No Breakfast Fallacy” — the conviction that once we’ve consumed today’s breakfast from the fridge, it is gone and there is consequently no more breakfast:
>
> Like the food in the fridge, “unsustainably” using up raw materials means that we run out of them. But also precisely like the food in the fridge, we replenish the raw materials we need, making “unsustainable” food consumption quite sustainable. How can this be?

> In that first instance we would agree with Worstall: eating breakfast does mean no breakfast in the fridge. We’d also agree that Worstall is mad because we understand that there is a vast industry dedicated solely to replenishing that breakfast before 7 am tomorrow.

> At any given time, there is some oil in storage, some proven (but not-yet-extracted) oil in the ground, some plausible pockets of oil and natural gas that geologists in various ventures are prospecting — and a big unknown chunk of oil reserves the amount and location of which nobody knows anything about. All of these actions (use, distribution, storage, extraction, prospecting) are governed and regulated by the market price of oil. If, as the resource depletion theory suggests, we would exhaust our known supplies of oil and raw materials, their market prices would rise — sending a palatable [signal to all market actors](https://mises.org/library/use-knowledge-society). Three things then happen:

![](https://m.stacker.news/159305)

***

Beautiful [graph](https://www.forbes.com/sites/rrapier/2025/07/08/global-oil-output-steady-but-subtle-shifts-hint-at-changes-ahead/) (a version of which I've cited before... https://stacker.news/items/1563548)

![](https://m.stacker.news/159302)

...the standard go-to energy report of the world has stopped reporting "proven reserves" which makes some sense on practical and methodological groups (too political, too uncertain too vague, too uneven cutoffs across countries).

In 2024, the world used 102m bpd of oil (*including* some coal and nat-gas derivatives), and when the EI (then BP) report last gave a figure for proven reserves (i.e., reserves that are known about and can be extracted given *current* financial and technological conditions), there was enough for 45 more years.

*No*, that doesn't mean by 2071 we're all fucked (sooner, really, because the oil consumption will rise... project that graph out 50-ish years), because *we will find and extract more*.

***

TL;DR:

> while we have a physically finite planet and a geologically limited amount of, say, [rare earth metals ](https://www.theverge.com/2019/5/23/18637071/rare-earth-china-production-america-demand-trade-war-tariffs)(or whatever the [latest fad ](https://capx.co/hollywoods-apocalypse-obsession-ignores-the-reality-of-human-progress/)of [environmental hysteria ](https://fee.org/articles/the-costs-of-hysteria/)may conjure up), the economic take-home point is that non-renewable resources actually [don’t run out](http://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/NaturalResources.html). In his hugely popular 1981 book *The Ultimate Resource*, Julian Simon forever changed the way a lot of people think about resources and raw materials. Simon pointed out that

## "Over the course of history, up to this very moment, copper and other minerals have been getting less scarce rather than more scarce, as the depletion theory implies … natural resources are not finite in any meaningful economic sense, mind-boggling though this assertion may be."
