items.title: A Suspicious Man
items.text:
A Suspicious Man

It was a scorching afternoon. Dawn trudged her way home, tired from a long day at school. When she reached her house, she saw something shocking. A well-built Chinese man was fiddling with the door handle of her neighbour’s house. Fear surged through her body.

	Dawn felt butterflies in her stomach. What if the suspicious man was a burglar? Without hesitation, she called her neighbour, Mrs Tan hastily. She wanted to warn Mrs Tan of the impending threat. She described the stranger’s features. Mrs Tan thanked Dawn for her concern, with a hint of a chuckle in her voice.

	Mrs Tan explained that she had been expecting her brother, so the man fiddling with the handle was most likely him. She opened the door and hugged him. Dawn also opened her door reluctantly. A mix of embarrassment and relief washed over her. She apologised to Mrs Tan profusely for making a mistake.

	In the end, Dawn learnt an important lesson. She would stay calm and not jump to conclusions in the future. She was grateful that no dreaded mishap had happened to Mrs Tan though!

items.title: Republicans feared a blue wave, but midterms could be a tsunami. Trumps failure.
items.text:
In some circles, concern about the elections goes beyond losing the House and Senate and into strongholds where Trump is having to campaign himself, writes Katy Balls, Washington Editor of The Times.

**ANALYSIS:** At a private members’ club in Washington one evening last week, a Republican strategist had a warning. “It’s as bad as everyone is whispering,” the strategist was told. “We’re about to see places we never thought could turn blue won by the Democrats. Afterwards, there is going to be \[a] reckoning.”

This is the new fear in Trumpworld: not just that the Republicans might lose control of the House and even the Senate come November, but that a “blue wave” is coming that will wipe out strongholds where the candidates are so comfortable they are not even used to campaigning.

So far much of the focus has been on the key battleground states, from Maine and Michigan to Texas and North Carolina, which will decide the balance of power in Washington. However, in recent weeks, some unexpected states have started to come up in conversation: Kansas, Oklahoma and Florida.

Given the last time the Democrats won in Kansas was 1932, Oklahoma was won by Donald Trump with 66% of the vote in 2024 and Florida is the Maga mecca of Mar-a-Lago, the idea that the party could have a fight on its hands in these red states is ringing serious alarm bells.

And why could it? The price of diesel in the US hit an all-time high of US$6.53 (NZ$11.54) per gallon last week. As the president rolled out the red carpet for President Xi of China, his approval rating fell. Voters are growing increasingly concerned about artificial intelligence and the economy.

“Where is the win right now?” asked one person in Trump’s orbit. “I can’t see it.” Instead the concern is that a president who rode to victory in 2024 pointing out the high cost of a dozen eggs - it had tripled compared with when Trump left office in 2021 - could be about to see his party smashed on rising prices.

Mention the “blue tsunami” to a Trump official and there is a common reply: fake news. The Republicans have surprised before, they argue, and will do so again. Chris LaCivita, a co-chair of Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, has taken to calling out journalists and pollsters spouting such ideas as clickbait chasers, losers and frauds.

![Chris La Civita, right, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, seen speaking with White House aide Natalie Harp, left, has taken to calling journalists and pollsters referring to a potential “blue tsunami” in the midterms “clickbait chasers, losers and frauds”, writes Katy Balls.](https://www.thepress.co.nz/media/images/9Tzi8ywRz924XE3uHaD6DZ3Ef+IdbOiYlvIROR5vlqUSeZYZbm+SU0zjMnNqDfql8Yk4r+Ht43oxrl86VwI5IF7k1TZFVP%2FGWCLS2aI+JHHuNPaop4flqU8q8GAZ%2FOSo%2FvTjUGdeaeSGU0y5nd1iJ57qLBNryQlorJmuzxCV2GdM6wTWOGyL+QaVDv1g1d9wFPVS0dueb7WH55BnyGuM%2FNjx0ghY1dtZR3pIYSAOWM2vgZX4cwgXZNK4slZ2296bqMKcBtrSVy573TxHRWPPTLG07DYixEqZplWalH5FS3Bd6C9+Ep5PW2yUmzgSwvGYOkiG9O7Fp64ySHQXbGxbm0HihE5V88Dt27tqDgJWm83qreCH6dgakmwfYZVO+c2TQyEKdIz6lQeudIN+qbEVBOgYn20rIHOHG7WrYQpH%2FEx0+Q7hq9tEE16XIH3DuzFJ4wo2pVOttm4XX%2FkqOJE5XJFv2WFjt45%2FDho4L7SR0fVkqVxTFxL9lVWlP07oDUN1Qw3ShiaPtM5ZtdLLqXhtqw==)

Chris La Civita, right, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, seen speaking with White House aide Natalie Harp, left, has taken to calling journalists and pollsters referring to a potential “blue tsunami” in the midterms “clickbait chasers, losers and frauds”, writes Katy Balls.Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP

But even if they are proven right and targeted campaigning, redistricting and a US$400m war chest come to the rescue, if you follow the money and the campaigns, it's clear the story playing out in the rest of the country is a stark contrast to the celebratory scenes last week in the White House.

There are three key tells. First, the messaging. In an appearance on the *All-In* podcast this month, JD Vance was asked what the administration’s closing message to voters would be before the midterms, just over a month away. He replied “give us another chance” before correcting himself to say “give us another couple of years” to keep doing great things.

But the implication was clear: rather than a rallying cry, Republicans are going to voters with their tails between their legs. There are conversations happening behind the scenes on how to approach voters fed up with a war that Maga promised not to start and that is pushing up prices. Members of the administration have been advising politicians to “level” with frustrated voters.

As Trump talks about a golden age, others, such as the vice-president, are saying “don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater”.

In an interview last week Vance was even asked about claims the result in November could be as bad as 2006, when George W Bush was president and backing an unpopular war, and his party lost the House and the Senate in the midterms. Vance insisted that this “worst nightmare” was not on the table as this administration has a much stronger policy record and the Democrats are further to the left than they were back then.

![Petrol and diesel prices displayed at a Shell service station in Doral, Florida on September 22. Diesel prices hit an all-time in the US last week.](https://www.thepress.co.nz/media/images/9Tzi8ywRz924XE3uHaD6DZ3Ef+IdbOiYlvIROR5vlqUSeZYZbm+SU0zjMnNqDfql8Yk4r+Ht43oxrl86VwI5IF7k1TZFVP%2FGWCLS2aI+JHFw5apxGAlsAlHDFCBwtFt20GEZnL6tb7zJv25noGOjtTo2qeElPH+x3KX76dp7SqijfIJMxv1nqk2GDqQIOzeERtJN9RgKEVKsiN0Yariet5tlMWNBNHGxQLNghivHPvH0Fq22DfnJUf0P63rI7h1FPUw56epWB%2F5xSp6EKQ+Xe18PapTNKUXXEE3So6ssMFS7tqRnFmpU0mBJ7JnlMcDTXna+y9T+MiKPRD1mCrJo6QanFXnUjId%2FPgog57cC9+Fzuk6tj49%2FOJFkb+mO0fcIwB13KOyUAxc38fdcVW%2FXqy3DWWEI2o3+T0USppHlw6zrzFM8q0pRT%2F4hm%2FxcFF49RMOfFlgVhxS8WmEfveQiyWcgAiI+5vgim52b1I2BhlPfNIBEANXTIYOkEQ%2FDyLiQ6N1lDY%2FuDgwQaVtaaLVxdz5guARgxAvDT%2Fq1ppwaF9Y=)

On Fox News, this has become the new way to campaign. The host Jesse Watters, who is one of Trump’s favourite journalists and attended the state banquet hosted for the Chinese president last week, put it like this: “Listen, am I excited about Susan Collins? Am I fired up about Rogers and Ken Paxton? Probably not, but the other side - a bunch of freaks. Maybe our side isn’t getting you very aroused but their side will kill the country.”

items.title: BOOK on BOOKS: "The Bushido of Bitcoin," by Alexandar Svetski
items.text:
We talked about Svetski returning to writing the other day (https://stacker.news/items/1578680), so it feels appropriate to run a Book on Books on his [*Bushido of Bitcoin*](https://link.amazon/B0b1pCmmX).

I remember the book fondly, and even though I'm not exactly a big fan of Japan (no hard feelings, just not interested), some of these virtues and historical anecdotes are nice. (I've been told in hindsight that much of Svetski's interpretation of Japanese/Samourai history is bonkers; I have no way of assessing it.) The subtitle is what we're really here to talk about... *A Moral Code for a World on a Bitcoin Standard*, a story of what happens when we win.

Of course, we haven't done too much winning lately, have we, so the hubris of a book like this was an early indication of a cycle top.

(This review was published in *Bitcoin Magazine* Print's [The Mining Issue](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/tags/the-mining-issue) in 2025, the mentioning of which was a condition of me republishing the reviews on SN.)

***

> I have been a fan of Svetski for years.

> Reading his work and seeing the scorn he receives from other Bitcoiners, I’ve often found myself in the confused position of Hamish Linklater’s character from the movie *The Big Short* — unable to “figure out why no one listened to Baum, the guy with all the good ideas”. A few years ago, it was an informal rule among us copy editors at *Bitcoin Magazine* to assign Svetski’s articles to me. I enjoyed them; the others couldn’t stand them.

> True, **Svetski is an acquired taste.** His writing is vertiginous and jarringly harsh. It’s uncompromising and so full of broad-brushed claims that readers will lose their way more than once, in this book as in many of his long-form articles. Even I, poised in his favor and inclined to agree with much of his thinking, can only stomach about a dozen pages at a time. Getting through the almost 350 pages of *Bushido* takes a while.

> Thus, if you have even the slightest of Svetski allergies, make a pledge to yourself to see through the antics of *Bushido*, the insults, and the topics where Svetski is likely to trigger you. Take seriously the idea that maybe — just maybe — there’s something deeper coming across these pages.

> It’s hard to summarize as wide a scope as that presented in *The Bushido of Bitcoin* since it tries to cover everything: from pre-modern Japanese virtues to Alexander the Great to the **origin of words, how to live well, and how Bitcoin brings back hierarchy and an appreciation for excellence to our times**. The cultural values of ancient civilizations belong in the modern world; over the last century we have lost many of those core virtues, and we are spiritually, socially, and morally poorer for it.

## "When the book isn’t radical, high-flying, or incoherent, it is dreamy."

> There is lots of Nietzsche and Spengler, Spartans and Ayn Rand. Much like Nietzschean philosophy itself, one has to sift through a lot of intricacies to get to Svetski’s worthwhile core. It flows like a History Channel episode mixed with a less eloquent version of Jordan Peterson, all wrapped in Japanese, Greek, and English etymology. Svetski longs for a different era — the past ages of kings and chivalry, or the future renaissance of such morals that *Bushido* predicts. Over the long arc of human civilization, today’s experiments in states and democracy, HR departments and central banks, are insignificant. In time, the cyclical forces that power them turn over — and the uncensorable hardness of Bitcoin ensures a world of strong men and good times.

## "Bushido, often translated as 'the way of the warrior', was the moral code governing the samurai in Japan’s Edo period";

> it gradually disappeared in the 1870s. *Bushido* tries to be a “playbook for a life on a Bitcoin Standard” (page 124); it’s how we live and behave when Bitcoin wins. Its battle isn’t Wall Street or retail or nation-state adoption, but the soul of humanity.

> The point with Bitcoin, and the reason Svetski writes about ancient ideas and societies and virtues for Bitcoiners is that “we now have a framework for excellence, which the ugly and deceitful cannot take advantage of” (page 316). Bitcoin isn’t value-neutral, he says; its adoption inspires changes “in domains such as food, family, self defense, knowledge, energy, shelter, health, masculine and feminine roles and much more” (page 142). It has, Svetski believes, “begun to transform the people who have come into contact with it”.

> Aside from the etymology, which he seems to have reproduced faithfully from widely accessible databases **(except “uni-verse”, where he bro-sciences us)**, he draws extensively on Inazo Nitobe’s century-old book *Bushido: The Soul of Japan*. Like most non-experts, I can’t gauge to what extent he has accurately portrayed the duties and values of a samurai, the workings of pre-modern Japan, or whether he’s playing fast and loose with the facts of ancient Greece or feudalist Europe. The reader has to trust him, which, given his otherwise aggressive and radical stances, they are unlikely to do.

> In the last third of the book he ruffles many feathers. One way or another, Svetski is going to annoy you — like when he claims female suffrage was **“quite possibly the greatest political mistake the West ever made” (page 56); “Women”, he writes, “are literally designed to bring life into the world**, and it is a man’s duty to create the frame and structure around her so she can do this safely and freely” (page 136).

## "By modern standards, he’s a fascist and a misogynist, a dangerous antidemocratic force and a mindless bigot."

> But Svetski doesn’t care for modern standards, rallying against them with all the bile of the self-righteous, purple-haired, queer academic he much despises. He is well aware of how unpalatable his ideas seem to others, but won’t budge: “If I’ve just pissed you all off, that’s fine too. Such is life, and such is exploration of ideas at the edge. This is where I choose to live, and I accept the consequences” (page 324).

> What he wants is to challenge you, not preach — though the text often feels like an endless hammering of precisely that. Still, he hopes that the book gives “a deeper appreciation and perspective of this ancient, sacred heritage of man” (page 13). 

> You don’t have to agree with everything Svetski says. But you must appreciate what he has created and the deep human vision he demands from a curious reader.

> Is Svetski right in all (any) of his ramblings, the coherent ones and wacky ones alike? Hardly. Could there still be some forgotten wisdom in the many past civilizations he surveys, something that our contemporary sensitivities, morals, and societies have ignored and discarded? Certainly.

> Only you can tell if wading through the former to find the latter is worth it.

***

**Selected quotes**

* “This is a book on behavior and the virtues we cannot ignore if our goal is to build a new and ascendant civilization. Who we become is determined by how we behave” (page 320)
* “The Samurai believed in doing, not saying. Action and behavior demonstrated their faith, knowledge and values, more than words ever could.” (46)
* “If you look back on the last century, we've had a steady rise of mental health issues, depression, and a plethora of syndromes and disorders - in lock step with the rise of 'psychology' both as a study and an institution. **We have come to ignore the body and the very things that make us alive.** We’ve drugged the feelings which are otherwise signals to act, into oblivion and replaced them with numbness and docility” (page 134)
* Money is a signaling network. It transmits information. But when the cables through which it operates are broken, rusted, or in our case elastic and obfuscated by the whims of a host of bureaucratic megalomaniacs, the information necessary to make decisions is completely distorted” (pages 238-39).

***

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Office of Cybersecurity Updated House Web and Cloud Security Affecting SN & Alby
items.text:
Over the last couple of weeks, I had been running into the oddest issue with SN, and I could not figure out for the life of me what was going on. On my personal laptop, whenever I would go to zap someone, the zap would fail, and I would get sent to a getalby.com webpage that would hit me with a "This site can't be reached" message. I was certain that this was an issue with my wallet connection, but after resetting them when I was at home the next day, the same issue occurred.

Now, with my attention fixed on trying to figure out what the hell was going on, I realized that whenever I would just type something in the address bar on Brave, I would get hit with a white page that said: "Your request has been refused by the server." Like a normal person I figured I either needed to update my computer or Brave itself and when I realized they were up to date the only thing I could think of at first was that I somehow broke my computer.

However, it still worked whenever I was hooked up to Wi-Fi that wasn't at work.... After a couple of days of trying to figure it out... it hit me. In August, before all of my travel, we had gotten an email about the House updating its internet.... Lo and behold, this "update" has tanked zapping and using Brave Search.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159324)

I talked with our IT guy, who confirmed it was likely these "upgrades" that have caused these issues. According to the House, now tipping on SN and using Brave Search is part of a high-risk website or unapproved cloud application. So sorry in advance for everyone who during the workday now gets CC from me as tips! I can't zap you sats anymore, and I actually have had to log into my work computer to zap posts since it does not interact with Alby at all. 

Gotta love the government making people "safer"

items.title: Another bitcoin adoption story
items.text:
Lately, I haven’t been able to find time for meetups because of family and work, so I decided to focus on lunches instead. In a regular local pub, I asked the owner if he’d be willing to accept Bitcoin. He politely declined.

I kept going there about once a week. After a few visits, I made an NFC card and loaded it with 1,000 sats as a tip. I also gave him a leaflet with instructions on how to access the Bitcoin. He’s an older gentleman, not very interested in technology, and doesn’t have much time for experiments while running the place. The following week, I tipped him another 1,000 sats. On the third week, he finally agreed to let me install a mobile wallet app for him.

Suddenly, he had a bit of Bitcoin in his Wallet of Satoshi. I asked him if I could start paying that way — with the promise that if it didn’t work out, I’d exchange it back into cash for him. He wasn’t too keen at first, but since I was a regular, he wanted to make me happy.

From that moment, I announced in the local Jednadvacet (our Czech version of Einundzwanzig) community that we’d meet for lunch every Thursday. A short meetup — a chance to exchange Bitcoin, learn something new, meet people, etc. The only condition: payment must be in Bitcoin.

Two months have passed since then. The group has been growing. At first, there were just three of us. Last time, there were already seventeen. For the owner, it’s become a significant part of that day’s revenue. He’s started treating us better too — now he greets us from afar and even reserves the biggest table for us every Thursday, not letting anyone else sit there.

Every time I ask him if everything’s okay, if he wants to cash out, or needs any help with it. And you know what he told me last time? That he doesn’t need to — it’s growing nicely in Bitcoin. He even recently bought a fridge with Bitcoin. He said he had to use Lightning because he ran into some issues with on-chain. I never even mentioned the word “Lightning” to him. He’s been learning on his own, and now he’s become quite the Bitcoiner.

It looks like the pub might soon turn into a nice little vexl point — a place where people can exchange Bitcoin for dirty fiat and vice versa.

I’m writing this because I think it’s a great blueprint. It’s short, takes me about an hour a week — time I’d spend on lunch anyway — I meet people, and it helps Bitcoin adoption in a very natural way. Hopefully, it’ll inspire more Bitcoiners to try something similar in their own area.

The chicken coop was battered by falling tree tops from recent heavy winds but the chicken compost system is still churning out compost and eggs.
![](https://i.nostr.build/QdKty1Cvs4sM5ptw.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/Bl2VhTfRzigPZBS3.jpg)
The 40ish birds are working 4 compost piles every day, breaking them down and consuming as many worms and fly larvae as the can find.
![](https://i.nostr.build/iNdM1gBA4b9vO85C.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/1FYWKfVTojZYynTg.jpg)
Each day I spend 20 minutes rebuilding the piles and watering them with nutrient rich water from the duck bath. Then I spend 20 minutes collecting as much fresh horse manure as I can, adding it to the system. With each rebuilding of the piles, they march slowly forward from the back of the paddock to the front. By the time the pile reaches the front the compost is finished and ready for use around the homestead. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/MbGXG22ZdoocGVU6.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/jh60ABOg7vAYpU2V.jpg)
While I do some work to maintain the energy flow through the system, the chickens are doing good work on the piles, consuming horse fly larvae reducing the pest pressure on the horses, and paying me in eggs for the work. Meanwhile I'm feeding them less and less grain. We are producing yeilds beyond what we can utilize at the homestead so I've been selling the compost and eggs at Bitcoin meetups in my area. Distributing natural capital and strengthening my local Bitcoin culture and community. A great example of a permaculture system here at the homestead!

items.title: Research in Public #20: Stacker News paper accepted at WISE 2026
items.text:
Almost exactly one year ago, I proposed to do a research paper using Stacker News data (https://stacker.news/items/1243188) and to do so in public, with all the code available in a public [github repo](https://github.com/ed-kung/sn-research), and regular public updates on the [progress of the research](https://stacker.news/SimpleStacker#research-in-public).

The first set of results were finished in around December 2025, and since then I've been trying to get it accepted at conferences and journals.  Unfortunately, the track record was not great.  A Bitcoin research conference did not take it (no reason given), the *Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization* did not take it (too niche), and *Electronics Commerce Research and Applications* did not take it (I don't write like an IS scholar).

But, I'm pleased to say that finally we are having some success. The paper was just accepted to the *Workshop on Information Systems and Economics*, which will be held in Lisbon, Portugal this December.  This is one of the main conferences for economists studying information systems, and the [program](https://wiseconf2026.github.io/) looks super interesting.  I think this is the right group of people to try and get this work in front of, and I'm looking forward to the feedback I get -- as well as the exposure Stacker News may receive from other researchers.

If you're interested, you can read a working draft of the paper [here](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6556022)

items.title: Bank Runs are Good, Actually: Death to the Central Banks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
ASTONISHING piece to see in regular financial press. *Maybe the tide is turning and the world is healing?*

![](https://m.stacker.news/159395)

The basic/most fundamental rationale for a central bank isn't financing the gov deficit (which they don't...*ish*) or set centralized interest rates, but to support commercial banks when faced with bank runs (=stand ready to lend against their assets, even if distressed, with newly created base money, so stave off the run.) The idea, from Francis Barings to Diamond\&Dybvig's [Nobel Prize](https://stacker.news/items/1583458?commentId=1583534) winning article, is that depositors are fickle and might/will run on perfectly healthy banks *and* that such runs cause real damage to the economy (*and* might spread through the banking system like wildfire and we all collapse into Great Depression 2.0).
*That's everything that's wrong with monetary economics and politics around central banks in one sentence...*

***

The authors of the paper Nangle discusses here used the Chronicling America project, scanned newspapers, then...

> they used LLMs to sift these articles further to find pieces about actual bank runs rather than, say, stuff about boats running into river banks, or the local bank manager running for mayor, and to match each report to individual banks.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159396)

> According to Verner, the research reveals that the idea that runs kill solvent banks is dramatically overstated. It turns out that depositors are actually pretty good at working out how dodgy a bank is, generally making runs on banks that are insolvent or very close to insolvent.

This is incredible. Specifically, — and I'm sparing you a deep dive into debates in financial history and monetary economics here — a big rationale for *why central banks must exist* is **to prevent bad types of bank runs.**

Running a bank means it has to shed assets, assets that aren't "finished," or turned into workable projects and thus liqudity, yet. (That's sort of the purpuse of a bank: to *liquify* illiquid assets, hold the maturity and duration mismatch in the meantime.)  Selling these assets quickly means taking (large) haircuts on book value, meaning a random run on a healthy bank can destroy projects or at least turn the bank itself bankrupt -- destroying customer relatioships and disrupting the bank-money-level money supply etc etc. 
**That's all unnecessary, and a benevolent central bank/observer can improve upon the state of the world by injecting more money and support the healthy bank.**

## ...except, depositors don't run on healthy banks!

That's what this beautiful history and database shows. Somehow, depositors (in aggregate) are clever enough to sniff out when something is wrong *and not* structurally/mindlessly/sunspot-style make erratic and concentrated mistakes.

If you scratch [the lender or last resort literature a little](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/when-did-the-bank-of-england-become-a-lender-of-last-resort/), you find that it's a good, disciplining market mechanism for depositors to run on banks. Here's a schematic:

* if bank is healthy and other bankers know it, then the bank can source enough liquidity from them ("recycling" deposits), against a very minimal short-term expense. **No problem, no negative outcome, no need for lender of last resort** 
* if the bank is unhealthy and the other bankers know it, they won't lend to it and it will fail, *and it will be a good thing!* Bankers taking bad risks or making bad investments should fail, like every other business in a market economy.
* if the bank is healthy, but the **other bankers don't know it** *and so refuse to lend*, that's when a lender of last resort needs to step in and save the day. By supplying that extra liquidity it can stave off the damaging run and everyone is better off for it.

Here's the best short article/overview I've ever seen on this (by [George Kaufman, for econlib](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/BankRuns.html)):

![](https://m.stacker.news/159394)

---

The literature on bank runs and central banks is basically an exercise in showing **whether or not the central bank knows about the true state of a given bank better than other bankers do.**

When central banks *also* had prudential obligation, by chance some of its workers would have recently audited and inspected private information for that bank, meaning it's quite plausible that central bankers *do* have some insider information here that they can act on. (Nowadays that function is usually separated to another agency, thus the argument is practically quite moot.)

But... If historically and practically depositors are good enough in aggregate to sniff out what's wrong, there's no *need* for a central bank to intervene and override their market choice.

Bank runs are bad for local economies

> ...only if the banks that are being abandoned have been making bad loans, a big borrower defaults, or something like that.

...in which case there is **a real economic loss that we want/need someone to carry** — not paper over and pretend it's not there. (\_cough\_, Bitfinex...)

***

Told yah:

> Surely **the mere process of a run on a healthy bank wreaked havoc on their local economy?** Apparently not.

> Cross-referencing each bank’s financial strength, the researchers trace the local economic impact of each bank run using Bradstreet’s contemporary reporting. They find that a run on a strong bank doesn’t really impose any economic cost at all on the local economy. Yet runs on banks whose fundamentals are awful are followed by major lending contractions that can cause all sorts of spillover problems.

and:

> Out of **3,984 bank runs on individual US banks from 1863–1934**, the authors identify 53 that look like they’re based on “misinformation” or “depositor confusion”, which reads as academese for “blind panic”. Of these 53 oddities, six banks failed, which sounds like maybe six too many. But the researchers argue that the historical data indicates that “strong banks (fundamentals in the upper tercile) subject to **non-fundamental runs have a zero probability of failure”**
> one of the footnotes indicates that at least one of these failed banks had basically committed massive fraud, which was only uncovered by their so-called irrational run.

*Even that*, the depositors sniffed out. Amazing.

***

All "pretty interesting" says Nangle, understating the explosive result.

> the ideas that the Nobel winners formalise are really the ones sitting behind the rationale for bank deposit insurance.

Yes. This evidence shows/weighs heavy that lender of last resort is a defunct and unnecessary function — liable to abuse, nepotism, and trigger-happy rulers, not actually saving a banking system that needs it

## Runs are good. Banks should fail more. And lender of last resort is an unnecessary function

items.title: How Private Are Bitcoin Transactions, Really? - Vinteum
items.text:
This is a pretty lengthy post, which has some echoes of slop, but which was also a nice survey of privacy in onchain bitcoin. The post is based on a five-day privacy focused retreat the Vinteum folks did. 

The post does a nice job of covering some of the concerns of onchain bitcoin, including chain analysis, wallet finger printing, and the asymmetrical nature of privacy: privacy must be constantly preserved, but one leak or mistake can have permanent consequences.

They cover payjoins and coinjoins and coinswaps and do a nice job of pointing out the strengths and weaknesses.

One particularly interesting note is that they mention something called the [Fungi Protocol](https://fungi-protocol.github.io/docs/) which looks to be a privacy project that Vinteum is working on. So far, the publicly available parts aren't very fleshed out, but it looks like they have a wallet-fingerprinting-blocker PSBT under development as well as some sort of collaborative spending technique. 

I'm curious to see what they make of Fungi. Definitely something to keep watching.

items.title: Nonrenewable Resources Never Truly Run Out (Mises Institute, JB)
items.text:
Recycling this beauty from 2019 for a very specific reason... I suppose ya'll will find out in a day or two

![](https://m.stacker.news/159301)

...as if I wasn't already on a mission to have the wokies and greenies *hate* my guts (https://stacker.news/items/1583743, https://stacker.news/items/1583533).

## Actually, "Renewable" is Bullshit and nonrenewable stuff never runs out

Here's the logic:

> In 1944 the world’s amount of proven oil reserves were 51bn barrels of oil. In 2018 the world’s proven oil reserves were almost 1,500bn (BP estimates [1,730](https://www.bp.com/en/global/corporate/energy-economics/statistical-review-of-world-energy/oil.html#oil-reserves)b[n ](https://www.bp.com/en/global/corporate/energy-economics/statistical-review-of-world-energy/oil.html#oil-reserves)), i.e., about thirty times that of 1944 — and this despite humanity’s pretty voracious appetite for oil during the seven-odd decades in between. Anyone immersed in the naïve resource depletion theory has to incredulously ask himself — *how can this be*?

> Simply put: we found more of it.

HOW?!

> In a trivial sense this is of course true: the anti-capitalist [environmentalists ](https://capx.co/the-totalitarianism-of-the-environmentalists/)are superficially correct about no [Planet B ](https://www.ecowatch.com/there-is-no-planet-b-1881704065.html)and the [impossibility of infinite growth of material consumption](https://www.brainyquote.com/quotes/e_f_schumacher_389554). But it’s also, as [Tim Worstall ](https://www.adamsmith.org/store/bzdlbo6oy071wbbz4v7fjgvoelr0ey)explains, **“supremely unimportant.”** In comparing the use of finite resources to food in the fridge, Worstall explodes the “No Breakfast Fallacy” — the conviction that once we’ve consumed today’s breakfast from the fridge, it is gone and there is consequently no more breakfast:
>
> Like the food in the fridge, “unsustainably” using up raw materials means that we run out of them. But also precisely like the food in the fridge, we replenish the raw materials we need, making “unsustainable” food consumption quite sustainable. How can this be?

> In that first instance we would agree with Worstall: eating breakfast does mean no breakfast in the fridge. We’d also agree that Worstall is mad because we understand that there is a vast industry dedicated solely to replenishing that breakfast before 7 am tomorrow.

> At any given time, there is some oil in storage, some proven (but not-yet-extracted) oil in the ground, some plausible pockets of oil and natural gas that geologists in various ventures are prospecting — and a big unknown chunk of oil reserves the amount and location of which nobody knows anything about. All of these actions (use, distribution, storage, extraction, prospecting) are governed and regulated by the market price of oil. If, as the resource depletion theory suggests, we would exhaust our known supplies of oil and raw materials, their market prices would rise — sending a palatable [signal to all market actors](https://mises.org/library/use-knowledge-society). Three things then happen:

![](https://m.stacker.news/159305)

***

Beautiful [graph](https://www.forbes.com/sites/rrapier/2025/07/08/global-oil-output-steady-but-subtle-shifts-hint-at-changes-ahead/) (a version of which I've cited before... https://stacker.news/items/1563548)

![](https://m.stacker.news/159302)

...the standard go-to energy report of the world has stopped reporting "proven reserves" which makes some sense on practical and methodological groups (too political, too uncertain too vague, too uneven cutoffs across countries).

In 2024, the world used 102m bpd of oil (*including* some coal and nat-gas derivatives), and when the EI (then BP) report last gave a figure for proven reserves (i.e., reserves that are known about and can be extracted given *current* financial and technological conditions), there was enough for 45 more years.

*No*, that doesn't mean by 2071 we're all fucked (sooner, really, because the oil consumption will rise... project that graph out 50-ish years), because *we will find and extract more*.

***

TL;DR:

> while we have a physically finite planet and a geologically limited amount of, say, [rare earth metals ](https://www.theverge.com/2019/5/23/18637071/rare-earth-china-production-america-demand-trade-war-tariffs)(or whatever the [latest fad ](https://capx.co/hollywoods-apocalypse-obsession-ignores-the-reality-of-human-progress/)of [environmental hysteria ](https://fee.org/articles/the-costs-of-hysteria/)may conjure up), the economic take-home point is that non-renewable resources actually [don’t run out](http://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/NaturalResources.html). In his hugely popular 1981 book *The Ultimate Resource*, Julian Simon forever changed the way a lot of people think about resources and raw materials. Simon pointed out that

## "Over the course of history, up to this very moment, copper and other minerals have been getting less scarce rather than more scarce, as the depletion theory implies … natural resources are not finite in any meaningful economic sense, mind-boggling though this assertion may be."

items.title: A Suspicious Man
items.text:
A Suspicious Man

It was a scorching afternoon. Dawn trudged her way home, tired from a long day at school. When she reached her house, she saw something shocking. A well-built Chinese man was fiddling with the door handle of her neighbour’s house. Fear surged through her body.

	Dawn felt butterflies in her stomach. What if the suspicious man was a burglar? Without hesitation, she called her neighbour, Mrs Tan hastily. She wanted to warn Mrs Tan of the impending threat. She described the stranger’s features. Mrs Tan thanked Dawn for her concern, with a hint of a chuckle in her voice.

	Mrs Tan explained that she had been expecting her brother, so the man fiddling with the handle was most likely him. She opened the door and hugged him. Dawn also opened her door reluctantly. A mix of embarrassment and relief washed over her. She apologised to Mrs Tan profusely for making a mistake.

	In the end, Dawn learnt an important lesson. She would stay calm and not jump to conclusions in the future. She was grateful that no dreaded mishap had happened to Mrs Tan though!

items.title: Republicans feared a blue wave, but midterms could be a tsunami. Trumps failure.
items.text:
In some circles, concern about the elections goes beyond losing the House and Senate and into strongholds where Trump is having to campaign himself, writes Katy Balls, Washington Editor of The Times.

**ANALYSIS:** At a private members’ club in Washington one evening last week, a Republican strategist had a warning. “It’s as bad as everyone is whispering,” the strategist was told. “We’re about to see places we never thought could turn blue won by the Democrats. Afterwards, there is going to be \[a] reckoning.”

This is the new fear in Trumpworld: not just that the Republicans might lose control of the House and even the Senate come November, but that a “blue wave” is coming that will wipe out strongholds where the candidates are so comfortable they are not even used to campaigning.

So far much of the focus has been on the key battleground states, from Maine and Michigan to Texas and North Carolina, which will decide the balance of power in Washington. However, in recent weeks, some unexpected states have started to come up in conversation: Kansas, Oklahoma and Florida.

Given the last time the Democrats won in Kansas was 1932, Oklahoma was won by Donald Trump with 66% of the vote in 2024 and Florida is the Maga mecca of Mar-a-Lago, the idea that the party could have a fight on its hands in these red states is ringing serious alarm bells.

And why could it? The price of diesel in the US hit an all-time high of US$6.53 (NZ$11.54) per gallon last week. As the president rolled out the red carpet for President Xi of China, his approval rating fell. Voters are growing increasingly concerned about artificial intelligence and the economy.

“Where is the win right now?” asked one person in Trump’s orbit. “I can’t see it.” Instead the concern is that a president who rode to victory in 2024 pointing out the high cost of a dozen eggs - it had tripled compared with when Trump left office in 2021 - could be about to see his party smashed on rising prices.

Mention the “blue tsunami” to a Trump official and there is a common reply: fake news. The Republicans have surprised before, they argue, and will do so again. Chris LaCivita, a co-chair of Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, has taken to calling out journalists and pollsters spouting such ideas as clickbait chasers, losers and frauds.

![Chris La Civita, right, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, seen speaking with White House aide Natalie Harp, left, has taken to calling journalists and pollsters referring to a potential “blue tsunami” in the midterms “clickbait chasers, losers and frauds”, writes Katy Balls.](https://www.thepress.co.nz/media/images/9Tzi8ywRz924XE3uHaD6DZ3Ef+IdbOiYlvIROR5vlqUSeZYZbm+SU0zjMnNqDfql8Yk4r+Ht43oxrl86VwI5IF7k1TZFVP%2FGWCLS2aI+JHHuNPaop4flqU8q8GAZ%2FOSo%2FvTjUGdeaeSGU0y5nd1iJ57qLBNryQlorJmuzxCV2GdM6wTWOGyL+QaVDv1g1d9wFPVS0dueb7WH55BnyGuM%2FNjx0ghY1dtZR3pIYSAOWM2vgZX4cwgXZNK4slZ2296bqMKcBtrSVy573TxHRWPPTLG07DYixEqZplWalH5FS3Bd6C9+Ep5PW2yUmzgSwvGYOkiG9O7Fp64ySHQXbGxbm0HihE5V88Dt27tqDgJWm83qreCH6dgakmwfYZVO+c2TQyEKdIz6lQeudIN+qbEVBOgYn20rIHOHG7WrYQpH%2FEx0+Q7hq9tEE16XIH3DuzFJ4wo2pVOttm4XX%2FkqOJE5XJFv2WFjt45%2FDho4L7SR0fVkqVxTFxL9lVWlP07oDUN1Qw3ShiaPtM5ZtdLLqXhtqw==)

Chris La Civita, right, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, seen speaking with White House aide Natalie Harp, left, has taken to calling journalists and pollsters referring to a potential “blue tsunami” in the midterms “clickbait chasers, losers and frauds”, writes Katy Balls.Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP

But even if they are proven right and targeted campaigning, redistricting and a US$400m war chest come to the rescue, if you follow the money and the campaigns, it's clear the story playing out in the rest of the country is a stark contrast to the celebratory scenes last week in the White House.

There are three key tells. First, the messaging. In an appearance on the *All-In* podcast this month, JD Vance was asked what the administration’s closing message to voters would be before the midterms, just over a month away. He replied “give us another chance” before correcting himself to say “give us another couple of years” to keep doing great things.

But the implication was clear: rather than a rallying cry, Republicans are going to voters with their tails between their legs. There are conversations happening behind the scenes on how to approach voters fed up with a war that Maga promised not to start and that is pushing up prices. Members of the administration have been advising politicians to “level” with frustrated voters.

As Trump talks about a golden age, others, such as the vice-president, are saying “don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater”.

In an interview last week Vance was even asked about claims the result in November could be as bad as 2006, when George W Bush was president and backing an unpopular war, and his party lost the House and the Senate in the midterms. Vance insisted that this “worst nightmare” was not on the table as this administration has a much stronger policy record and the Democrats are further to the left than they were back then.

Even Trump seems to be preparing for the worst. At the UN general assembly last week, he distanced himself from the ballot, saying: "They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don't realise is that I'm not running. I did that already and won in a landslide." He added that he would be around whatever happens: "I'll be here for two and a half years."

Next, the money. This week Trump will speak at rallies in Alabama and Oklahoma. The idea had been for the president to embark on a midterm tour of battleground states, but instead he’s visiting two of the most Republican states in the country. It's not just because he might appreciate a stop with a warm reception.

The Republicans have made much of their war chest, but some of these funds have started being diverted to red states. “We should have pulled Ohio funding already,” says one Republican strategist. “We now need to spend to hold safe ground.”

In Iowa, a Maga talk show host and local Steve Deace posted on X last week: "Yesterday (Saturday), Iowa House Republicans were informed by their own pollsters that if you are in a +15 district \[expected to win by a 15 per cent point margin], you're within the margin for error, if you're in a +10 district you're underwater, and that this might end being an even worse midterm environment than 2006."

A Republican working on election strategy said: "It might not look as bad on the surface at the congressional level because of the redistricting but ... it's going to be pretty rough when you look at real net loss."

Finally, listen to the candidates themselves. In the first year of Trump's presidency, Congress was notably supine. One time "Never Trumpers" either left the field or contorted into new positions.

But all of a sudden they seem to be finding their voices. Last week, the Republicans running for the Senate in Michigan and Iowa called on the president to end the war in Iran.

Ashley Hinson, in Iowa, whose agriculture-heavy state is particularly hurt by diesel costs, called on politicians to suspend gas taxes, adding "the \[Iran] war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end". The message was echoed by Mike Rogers in Michigan.

In Florida, the Republican candidate for governor, Byron Donalds, has been accused of revamping his website to make his Trump endorsement less prominent. Floridians say one of their biggest issues will be if the Hispanic vote turns away from Trump over Immigration and Customs Enforcement checks they view as overly harsh.

Last week, Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida - who represents a district Trump won with 57 per cent of the vote - released a new advert where she spoke to Trump about immigration.

Few Republicans expect Trump to come to their rescue. Instead, they think he will do what he wants, whether it's praising AI in the face of voter hesitation and anger over data centres, or continuing the war.

items.title: BOOK on BOOKS: "The Bushido of Bitcoin," by Alexandar Svetski
items.text:
We talked about Svetski returning to writing the other day (https://stacker.news/items/1578680), so it feels appropriate to run a Book on Books on his [*Bushido of Bitcoin*](https://link.amazon/B0b1pCmmX).

I remember the book fondly, and even though I'm not exactly a big fan of Japan (no hard feelings, just not interested), some of these virtues and historical anecdotes are nice. (I've been told in hindsight that much of Svetski's interpretation of Japanese/Samourai history is bonkers; I have no way of assessing it.) The subtitle is what we're really here to talk about... *A Moral Code for a World on a Bitcoin Standard*, a story of what happens when we win.

Of course, we haven't done too much winning lately, have we, so the hubris of a book like this was an early indication of a cycle top.

(This review was published in *Bitcoin Magazine* Print's [The Mining Issue](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/tags/the-mining-issue) in 2025, the mentioning of which was a condition of me republishing the reviews on SN.)

***

> I have been a fan of Svetski for years.

> Reading his work and seeing the scorn he receives from other Bitcoiners, I’ve often found myself in the confused position of Hamish Linklater’s character from the movie *The Big Short* — unable to “figure out why no one listened to Baum, the guy with all the good ideas”. A few years ago, it was an informal rule among us copy editors at *Bitcoin Magazine* to assign Svetski’s articles to me. I enjoyed them; the others couldn’t stand them.

> True, **Svetski is an acquired taste.** His writing is vertiginous and jarringly harsh. It’s uncompromising and so full of broad-brushed claims that readers will lose their way more than once, in this book as in many of his long-form articles. Even I, poised in his favor and inclined to agree with much of his thinking, can only stomach about a dozen pages at a time. Getting through the almost 350 pages of *Bushido* takes a while.

> Thus, if you have even the slightest of Svetski allergies, make a pledge to yourself to see through the antics of *Bushido*, the insults, and the topics where Svetski is likely to trigger you. Take seriously the idea that maybe — just maybe — there’s something deeper coming across these pages.

> It’s hard to summarize as wide a scope as that presented in *The Bushido of Bitcoin* since it tries to cover everything: from pre-modern Japanese virtues to Alexander the Great to the **origin of words, how to live well, and how Bitcoin brings back hierarchy and an appreciation for excellence to our times**. The cultural values of ancient civilizations belong in the modern world; over the last century we have lost many of those core virtues, and we are spiritually, socially, and morally poorer for it.

## "When the book isn’t radical, high-flying, or incoherent, it is dreamy."

> There is lots of Nietzsche and Spengler, Spartans and Ayn Rand. Much like Nietzschean philosophy itself, one has to sift through a lot of intricacies to get to Svetski’s worthwhile core. It flows like a History Channel episode mixed with a less eloquent version of Jordan Peterson, all wrapped in Japanese, Greek, and English etymology. Svetski longs for a different era — the past ages of kings and chivalry, or the future renaissance of such morals that *Bushido* predicts. Over the long arc of human civilization, today’s experiments in states and democracy, HR departments and central banks, are insignificant. In time, the cyclical forces that power them turn over — and the uncensorable hardness of Bitcoin ensures a world of strong men and good times.

## "Bushido, often translated as 'the way of the warrior', was the moral code governing the samurai in Japan’s Edo period";

> it gradually disappeared in the 1870s. *Bushido* tries to be a “playbook for a life on a Bitcoin Standard” (page 124); it’s how we live and behave when Bitcoin wins. Its battle isn’t Wall Street or retail or nation-state adoption, but the soul of humanity.

> The point with Bitcoin, and the reason Svetski writes about ancient ideas and societies and virtues for Bitcoiners is that “we now have a framework for excellence, which the ugly and deceitful cannot take advantage of” (page 316). Bitcoin isn’t value-neutral, he says; its adoption inspires changes “in domains such as food, family, self defense, knowledge, energy, shelter, health, masculine and feminine roles and much more” (page 142). It has, Svetski believes, “begun to transform the people who have come into contact with it”.

> Aside from the etymology, which he seems to have reproduced faithfully from widely accessible databases **(except “uni-verse”, where he bro-sciences us)**, he draws extensively on Inazo Nitobe’s century-old book *Bushido: The Soul of Japan*. Like most non-experts, I can’t gauge to what extent he has accurately portrayed the duties and values of a samurai, the workings of pre-modern Japan, or whether he’s playing fast and loose with the facts of ancient Greece or feudalist Europe. The reader has to trust him, which, given his otherwise aggressive and radical stances, they are unlikely to do.

> In the last third of the book he ruffles many feathers. One way or another, Svetski is going to annoy you — like when he claims female suffrage was **“quite possibly the greatest political mistake the West ever made” (page 56); “Women”, he writes, “are literally designed to bring life into the world**, and it is a man’s duty to create the frame and structure around her so she can do this safely and freely” (page 136).

## "By modern standards, he’s a fascist and a misogynist, a dangerous antidemocratic force and a mindless bigot."

> But Svetski doesn’t care for modern standards, rallying against them with all the bile of the self-righteous, purple-haired, queer academic he much despises. He is well aware of how unpalatable his ideas seem to others, but won’t budge: “If I’ve just pissed you all off, that’s fine too. Such is life, and such is exploration of ideas at the edge. This is where I choose to live, and I accept the consequences” (page 324).

> What he wants is to challenge you, not preach — though the text often feels like an endless hammering of precisely that. Still, he hopes that the book gives “a deeper appreciation and perspective of this ancient, sacred heritage of man” (page 13). 

> You don’t have to agree with everything Svetski says. But you must appreciate what he has created and the deep human vision he demands from a curious reader.

> Is Svetski right in all (any) of his ramblings, the coherent ones and wacky ones alike? Hardly. Could there still be some forgotten wisdom in the many past civilizations he surveys, something that our contemporary sensitivities, morals, and societies have ignored and discarded? Certainly.

> Only you can tell if wading through the former to find the latter is worth it.

***

**Selected quotes**

* “This is a book on behavior and the virtues we cannot ignore if our goal is to build a new and ascendant civilization. Who we become is determined by how we behave” (page 320)
* “The Samurai believed in doing, not saying. Action and behavior demonstrated their faith, knowledge and values, more than words ever could.” (46)
* “If you look back on the last century, we've had a steady rise of mental health issues, depression, and a plethora of syndromes and disorders - in lock step with the rise of 'psychology' both as a study and an institution. **We have come to ignore the body and the very things that make us alive.** We’ve drugged the feelings which are otherwise signals to act, into oblivion and replaced them with numbness and docility” (page 134)
* Money is a signaling network. It transmits information. But when the cables through which it operates are broken, rusted, or in our case elastic and obfuscated by the whims of a host of bureaucratic megalomaniacs, the information necessary to make decisions is completely distorted” (pages 238-39).

***

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Office of Cybersecurity Updated House Web and Cloud Security Affecting SN & Alby
items.text:
Over the last couple of weeks, I had been running into the oddest issue with SN, and I could not figure out for the life of me what was going on. On my personal laptop, whenever I would go to zap someone, the zap would fail, and I would get sent to a getalby.com webpage that would hit me with a "This site can't be reached" message. I was certain that this was an issue with my wallet connection, but after resetting them when I was at home the next day, the same issue occurred.

Now, with my attention fixed on trying to figure out what the hell was going on, I realized that whenever I would just type something in the address bar on Brave, I would get hit with a white page that said: "Your request has been refused by the server." Like a normal person I figured I either needed to update my computer or Brave itself and when I realized they were up to date the only thing I could think of at first was that I somehow broke my computer.
